title: Identifying Scientifically Interesting Galaxies with Vision-Language Models
authors: Yixuan Cheng, Nolan Koblischke, Jo Bovy
abstract: Anomaly searches in large astronomical image datasets aim to identify rare objects for follow-up investigation. Yet the objects that are most statistically unusual are not necessarily those of greatest scientific relevance. We investigate whether pretrained vision-language models can directly assess scientific interest from natural-language instructions, enabling galaxy images to be ranked without labeled examples. We evaluate models on a 20,000-image Hubble Space Telescope sample that includes 167 reference anomalies previously identified through machine learning and expert inspection. By scoring images for scientific interest, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite places 98.2% of the reference anomalies within the highest-ranked ~2,000 images, at a present-day inference cost of approximately $5.05 per 10,000 images. We recover known gravitational lenses, jellyfish-galaxy candidates, and galaxies with visible jets, and release 102 high-scoring candidates for further investigation. These results show that an off-the-shelf vision-language model, without any training on the target data, offers a practical way to rank large image datasets by scientific relevance rather than rarity. The project code is available at this https URL
comments: Accepted to the Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop (ML4PS 2026)

title: A GLIMPSE of Dark Matter: JWST Constraints on Early Structure Formation
authors: Julian B. Muñoz, John Chisholm, Seiji Fujimoto, Tiger Yu-Yang Hsiao, Kristen B. W. McQuinn, Priyamvada Natarajan, A. Saldana-Lopez, Hakim Atek, Arghyadeep Basu, Danielle Berg, Ryan Endsley, Lukas J. Furtak, Damien Korber, Rohan P. Naidu, Richard Pan, Daniel Schaerer
abstract: While we have a solid understanding of how dark matter (DM) behaves during recombination ($z\sim 10^3$) and in the late universe ($z\lesssim$ a few), much less is known about intermediate times, when the first galaxies formed. These galaxies provide a powerful handle on DM through structure formation, as halos have to exist to host luminous sources. Here we use recent determinations of the UV luminosity function from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) GLIMPSE lensing program, along with legacy Hubble and Subaru data, to test the small-scale behavior of DM during the epoch of reionization ($z\sim 7$). Marginalizing over astrophysical uncertainties, we find the matter power spectrum to be consistent with the cold-DM prediction down to sub-Mpc scales, with 1$\sigma$ uncertainties of 0.2 dex at $k=3-9 \, \rm Mpc^{-1}$ and 0.5 dex at $k=9-27 \, \rm Mpc^{-1}$, the smallest scales probed at these early times. For thermal-relic warm DM we constrain $m_{\rm WDM} > 3.2\, \rm keV$ (95% CL), independent of lower-$z$ probes. Our results test small-scale structure formation in a new redshift window and demonstrate the promise of JWST to constrain the nature of DM.
comments: 7+1 pages, 3+1 figures, comments welcome

figs.cap: The matter power spectrum $P(k)$ linearly extrapolated to $z=0$. Black line is the CDM prediction and red dashed is WDM with $m_{\rm WDM}=3.2$ keV (at our 95% CL). Colored circles show measurements from different probes [33, 5, 111, 91, 2], and vertical green-dotted lines correspond to the non-linear scale (defined as $k_{\rm NL}=1/R_{\rm NL}$ for the radius $R_{\rm NL}$ that has unit variance) at $z\sim 0,~4$ and $7$. Our results are shown as black squares, which reach comparable scales to strong lensing [51, purple region] but at higher $z$, and smaller scales (higher $k$, smaller halo masses on the top axis) than past UVLF work with HST [95, gray].

UVLF at $z\sim 7$ predicted within CDM (solid), WDM (with $m_{\rm WDM}=3.2$ keV, red dashed), and a model with a 2$\times$ reduction in power for $k\geq 9\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ (orange dotted), alongside data from HST-blank fields (yellow circles), HST-lens (blue squares), and JWST’s GLIMPSE (green diamonds). The depth of GLIMPSE allows us to better constrain small-scale structure and thus deviations from CDM.

Posterior for the (inverse) WDM mass for different datasets. Adding GLIMPSE (green) tightens the 2$\sigma$ limit (vertical dashed lines), reaching $m_{\rm WDM}>3.2$ keV, the strongest reionization-era limit to date.

Uncertainties of different UVLF datasets are shown as shaded regions.

title: Disentangling constraints on $S_8$ from the high and low redshift CMB
authors: Joann Jones, Ualype de Andrade Uchôa, Scott Dodelson
abstract: The clustering of matter in the universe is quantified by $\sigma_8$, the RMS fluctuations today in linear theory in spheres of radius $8h^{-1}$ Mpc, where $h$ parametrizes the Hubble constant. Surveys of gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering best constrain $S_8\equiv (\Omega_m/0.3)^{0.5} \sigma_8$, where $\Omega_m$ is the energy density of matter in units of the critical density. Comparing this late time measurement to the value of $S_8$ inferred from the cosmic microwave background (CMB), one can test the $\Lambda$CDM prediction for the growth of clustering from the primordial universe to now. Several analyses report hints that CMB measurements of $S_8$ are larger than those from galaxy surveys. However, CMB measurements have information from both high and low redshift due to lensing, and these tests traditionally conflate the two. Here, we present a technique to extract constraints on the cosmological parameters from each redshift component separately, enabling a high-z vs. low-z clustering comparison that was not previously possible. We marginalize over lensing information using a principal component analysis, and show that the primordial CMB from combined Planck 2018, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 prefers $S_8= 0.795\pm0.022$, in agreement with the recent determination from the Dark Energy Survey (DES) of $S_8=0.789\pm0.012$. The clustering inferred from CMB lensing is larger. However, both the level of excess lensing and increase in agreement with DES depends on the prior on the sum of neutrino masses, $\sum m_\nu$. We find that removing lensing brings the CMB towards agreement with DES in any case.
comments: 9 pages, 5 figures

figs.cap: Constraints on the physical matter density, $\omega_{bc}\equiv(\Omega_{b}+\Omega_{c})h^{2}$ and $S_{8}$ (68% and 95% credible regions). The CMB 2-pt constraint from Planck 2018, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 (purple) is in mild tension with the DES Year 6 $3\times 2$pt result at $0.3<z^{\rm GS}<1$ (green) [1]. The unlensed CMB (red), with the lensing smoothing marginalized over two principal components, measures clustering at $z_{*}$ and is consistent with DES. CMB lensing from the 4-pt function (blue) measures clustering at $0.7<z^{\rm CMBL}<5$ and prefers the higher $S_{8}$ of the CMB 2-pt result. Presented with $S_{8}^{\text{CMBL}}$ in Appendix A.

Constraints on $S_{8}$ (mean and 68% interval), labeled by the redshift each probe measures. The shaded band shows the DES Year 6 $3\times 2$pt $1\sigma$ interval at $0.3<z^{\rm GS}<1$. The two unlensed CMB rows measure clustering from information at $z_{*}$. One marginalizes the lensing smoothing over two principal components, the other marginalizes over the amplitude $A_{L}$. Both agree with DES. CMB lensing from the 4-pt function infers the amount of clustering from $0.7<z^{\rm CMBL}<5$ and prefers a higher $S_{8}$, as does the CMB 2-pt result, which combines information from both epochs. See Appendix A for results presented in $S_{8}^{\text{CMBL}}.$

title: Seeing Unseen Gravitational Wave Inspirals at the Galactic Center
authors: Pau Amaro Seoane, Qimin Song, Shao-Dong Zhao, Kostas Tzanavaris, Reinhard Genzel, Frank Eisenhauer, Thomas Ott, Stefan Gillessen, Guillaume Bourdarot, Diogo C. Ribeiro, Matteo Sadun Bordoni, Simran Joharle, Felix Mang, Andreas Burkert, Jorge Cuadra, Diego Calderón, Re'em Sari
abstract: The Galactic Center is expected to host a population of extremely large mass-ratio inspirals (X-MRIs) migrating toward the supermassive black hole. We propose an observational approach utilizing the secular gravitational torque exerted by X-MRIs on the highly eccentric S-star S301. This approach is intrinsically limited by the stochastic nature of the surrounding stellar-mass black hole cusp. As S301 propagates through this granular medium, it experiences discrete gravitational encounters. Standard orbital fitting procedures inherently assume a smooth background potential; applying them to stochastic trajectories averages these discrete velocity discontinuities into a continuous secular drift. This introduces a systematic bias that mimics the X-MRI precession signal, invalidating traditional mass estimation techniques. To resolve this degeneracy, we implement a methodology based on the Wavelet Transform Modulus Maxima method to characterize the local Hölder regularity of the orbital motion. This model isolates the singular discontinuities induced by stellar-mass black hole encounters from the continuous torque of the X-MRI distribution, allowing for detection even when instantaneous accelerations are below the instrumental noise threshold. We demonstrate analytically that S301 is highly sensitive to the interior X-MRI population while remaining dynamically decoupled from the secular influence of the exterior cusp. Combining precision astrometry and radial velocity projections, we establish that a minimal population of two X-MRIs is detectable within a five to nine-year timeframe, allowing us to constrain the presence of an unseen orbiter population prior to the launch of space-based gravitational wave detectors.
comments: Accepted for publication ApJ Letters

figs.cap: Trajectories of all celestial bodies, including Sgr A*, 38 S-stars and 2 BDs. The coordinate origin is defined at the initial position of Sgr A*. The inset provides a zoomed-in view of the trajectories of S301 and the two BDs.

Evolutionary trajectories of the system comprising Sgr A*, S301, and two BDs. All components are initialized as coplanar (apparent out-of-plane separation is due to the 3D perspective projection and minor out-of-plane perturbations from the 37 background S-stars over 35 years).

Distribution of the absolute precession residuals for S301 $|\dot{\omega}|$ in the misalignment case, which are predominantly concentrated between 0.1 and 10 $\mathrm{arcsec\,yr}^{-1}$ as well.

title: Thinner Disks Struggle to Launch Jets: GRMHD Simulations of Magnetic Field Generation and Transport
authors: Jonatan Jacquemin-Ide, Mitchell C. Begelman, Henrik Latter, Jason Dexter, Alexander Tchekhovskoy
abstract: Relativistic jets are observed in some accreting black-hole systems but not others. In X-ray binaries, jet production is closely associated with geometrically thicker accretion states, suggesting that disk thickness may influence the conditions for jet launching. We investigate this connection using three-dimensional GRMHD simulations of disks with $h/r=0.1$--$0.3$, initialized with a toroidal magnetic field with plasma $\beta=5$. We find that the magnetorotational instability (MRI) generates large-scale poloidal fields through non-axisymmetric shearing waves, with an additional contribution from axisymmetric induction through stretching by channel-like modes. The resulting mean fields become progressively weaker as the disk becomes thinner. Because these fields regulate MRI turbulence, thinner disks exhibit weaker angular-momentum transport and accrete more slowly than the standard $v_{\rm acc}\propto(h/r)^2$ thin-disk scaling would predict. The magnetic-flux transport velocity remains comparable to the accretion velocity, so weaker field generation and slower transport combine to strongly suppress black-hole flux accumulation at smaller $h/r$. Correspondingly, the thinnest disk ($h/r=0.1$) produces an electromagnetic jet efficiency of only $\eta_{\rm{EM}}\sim1\%$, while the thickest disk reaches the magnetically arrested disk (MAD) state and attains $\eta_{\rm{EM}}\geq100\%$. Using the measured large-scale magnetic flux distribution and transport velocities, we estimate the time required to accumulate MAD-level magnetic flux. Only the $h/r\sim0.3$ disk reaches MAD in the duration of our simulations, at $t\simeq2\times10^4\,r_g/c$, whereas for $h/r=0.1$ we estimate a timescale of $\sim10^8\,r_g/c$. These results link disk geometry to magnetic-flux accumulation and jet launching, with direct implications for the timescales over which jets can emerge in transient accreting systems.
comments: Submitted to MNRAS comments welcomed

figs.cap: Black-hole magnetic flux and jet evolution for the three disk thicknesses. Panel (a) shows the MADness parameter, $\phi_{\rm BH}$, with only the thickest disk reaching the MAD state during the simulation. Panel (b) shows the signed horizon-threading magnetic flux, normalized by its maximum absolute value in each simulation, with all three cases undergoing at least one polarity reversal. Panel (c) shows the electromagnetic jet efficiency, $\eta_{\rm EM}$, measured at the black-hole horizon. For the $h/r\sim 0.3$ simulation, regions shown in lighter colours indicate intervals where the data were reconstructed from the available reduced quantities. Both magnetic-flux accumulation and jet efficiency decrease strongly with decreasing disk thickness.

Temporal evolution of the inverse plasma betas associated with the turbulent, mean toroidal, and mean poloidal magnetic fields at $r=20r_{g}$, shown in units of the shear timescale $\Omega_{k}^{-1}$ for $h/r\sim 0.3$ (a), $0.2$ (b), and $0.1$ (c). All simulations show rapid exponential growth of the turbulent and mean poloidal fields, followed by relaxation toward a statistical quasi-steady state. The saturated fields satisfy $\left\langle\delta B^{2}\right\rangle\gg\left\langle B_{\varphi}\right\rangle^{2}\gg\left\langle B_{p}\right\rangle^{2}$, with the separation between the mean toroidal and poloidal components increasing toward thinner disks.

Vertical profiles of the toroidal magnetic-energy budget at $r=20r_{g}$ for $h/r\sim 0.3$ (a), $0.2$ (b), and $0.1$ (c), showing the shear, mean-advection, and turbulent terms from Eq. 23, together with their sum and $\frac{1}{2}\partial_{t}\left\langle B_{\varphi}^{2}\right\rangle$. The close agreement between the latter two quantities indicates a local quasi-steady balance. Shear generates toroidal magnetic energy, while turbulent and axisymmetric terms remove it. In the thinner disks, both generation and dissipation are suppressed near the midplane and become concentrated around $|z|\sim 3h$.

Normalized spectrum of the poloidal-field generation term, $\delta\mathcal{A}_{p}^{(m)}$, as a function of azimuthal wavelength $\lambda_{\varphi}/h$ at $r=20r_{g}$. Panels show averages over the full vertical region (a), the disk midplane (b), and the disk atmosphere (c). Large-scale modes with $\lambda_{\varphi}>\lambda_{I}$ generate poloidal magnetic field in both regions, intermediate modes with $\lambda_{S}<\lambda_{\varphi}<\lambda_{I}$ generate field within the disk but dissipate it in the atmosphere, and small-scale modes with $\lambda_{\varphi}<\lambda_{S}$ dissipate the field in both regions. The characteristic transition wavelengths $\lambda_{I}$ and $\lambda_{S}$ are shown as vertical dashed lines and are similar across disk thicknesses when normalized by $h$, indicating that the dynamo scale hierarchy is set primarily by the local disk thickness.

Radial profiles of the temporally averaged accretion velocity, $v_{\rm acc}$, and magnetic-flux transport velocity, $v_{\Phi}$, normalized by the Keplerian velocity, for $h/r\sim 0.3$ (a), $0.2$ (b), and $0.1$ (c). The dotted horizontal lines show the prediction from the angular-momentum transport model, which agrees well with the measured $v_{\rm acc}$ at $r\gtrsim 10r_{g}$. The flux transport velocity remains comparable to the accretion velocity in all simulations, and both decrease steeply as the disk becomes thinner.

Spacetime evolution of the signed magnetic flux, $\Phi(r,t)$, for $h/r=0.3$ (a), $0.2$ (b), and $0.1$ (c). Colours indicate magnetic polarity and contours trace magnetic flux surfaces as they evolve through the disk. In all simulations, progressively larger magnetic loops are generated and advected inward, producing a coherent large-scale flux structure at late times. The dotted black curves traces representative magnetic flux surfaces identified in the simulation, while the solid black lines show a corresponding analytical trajectories. The agreement deteriorates at small radii ($r\leq 5r_{g}$), where ISCO and near-horizon dynamics are not captured by the simple transport model. The markedly slower transport in thinner disks explains their correspondingly slower black-hole flux accumulation.

title: Extreme eccentricity in double neutron stars without exotic physics
authors: Thomas M. Tauris
abstract: The formation of neutron stars (NSs) underpins astrophysical phenomena from supernovae (SNe), radio pulsars and X-ray binaries to double NS mergers that power gravitational waves (GWs), short gamma-ray bursts and r-process kilonovae. A recently reported double NS (PSR J0653+0443) with record eccentricity e=0.9924 provides a unique laboratory for studying GW emission and orbital evolution, and challenges existing formation scenarios. Here we show that such extreme eccentricities arise naturally -- without invoking exotic conditions -- from standard binary-SN physics: instantaneous mass loss (Blaauw recoil) and natal kicks readily produce e>0.99 for both compact and wide pre-SN orbits. The observed orbit matches three families of kinematic solutions spanning a range of kick velocities and progenitor configurations. Physically motivated priors based on NS spin and pre-SN mass transfer constrain the viable progenitor family, demonstrating that the system is not exceptionally rare. Future proper-motion measurements will tightly constrain its natal SN kick magnitude.
comments: Nature Astronomy, accepted August 14, 2026 (submitted April 11, 2026). This author's version differs slightly from the accepted manuscript. 55 pages, 16 figures, 3 tables (including Supplementary Information)

figs.cap: Figure 1 Past and future orbital and spin evolution of PSR J0653+0443. Past ($t<0$) and future ($t>0$) evolution of the semi-major axis (top-left panel), eccentricity (top-right panel), and periastron separation (lower-left panel; note the “frozen-pericenter” effect). The current system is marked by a solid star at $t=0$. The spin evolution (lower-right panel) is shown for three braking indices, $n=\{2,3,5\}$ until the system will merge in 2.54 Gyr due to GW emission (shaded region). The spin-down age $\tau=6.58\;{\rm Gyr}$ (Supplementary Information Section D) is indicated by an arrow in all panels, although the true age likely differs from $\tau$. For DNSs, tidal and spin–orbit effects are negligible, and significant external torques are unlikely given the Galactic-field location of PSR J0653+0443.

Figure 2 Three families of kinematic solutions. Three families of progenitor models (T, K and W; colour coded) emerge from SN simulations reproducing the orbital properties of the extremely eccentric DNS PSR J0653+0443. The tight (T) progenitors have pre-SN orbital periods $P_{0}<0.2\;{\rm days}$ and kicks $w<500\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$. The wide (W) progenitors span $0.2\leq P_{0}<240\;{\rm days}$ and show an anti-correlation between $P_{0}$ and $w$, with $w<500\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$. The very large-kick (K) progenitors require $w>500\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$ and $0.035<P_{0}<1.7\;{\rm days}$. The green circle at $w=0$ marks a symmetric SN. Progenitor systems with $P_{0}>P=79.1\;{\rm days}$ (arrow) are shown in dark blue and were kicked inward. All models span exploding-star masses $M_{\rm He,f}=1.60–4.40\;M_{\odot}$; see Extended Data Figs. 2–5 for further details and tighter constraints based on physically motivated priors.

Figure 3 Recycling of first-born NS. The spin period of the recycled pulsar depends on the amount of material accreted from the progenitor of the exploding star prior to the SN. Efficient recycling (see direction of arrow and Supplementary Information Section C) to $P_{\rm spin}\lesssim 50\;{\rm ms}$ is expected in NS+He star systems with initially low-mass He-stars ($\lesssim 3.2\;M_{\odot}$) in tight binaries. The final exploding star is efficiently stripped down to $M_{\rm He,f}\leq 2.0\;M_{\odot}$, giving rise to an ultra-stripped SN explosion[10] where little baryonic material ($\sim 0.1-0.5\;M_{\odot}$) is ejected. The data are taken from Table 1 of ref. 10. Each data point is colour-coded according to expected spin period after recycling and its area scales with initial He-star mass ($2.8-10\;M_{\odot}$) prior to mass transfer.

Figure 4 Correlation between kick velocity and systemic velocity. Diagnostic plot showing the near one-to-one correlation between the magnitudes of SN kick velocity, $w$, and the current systemic velocity, $v_{\rm sys}$, of PSR J0653+0443. Simulations are drawn from Extended Data Fig. 5 and are based on “realistic” binary-stellar evolution modelling. For comparison, the green circle at $w=0$ marks the resulting value $v_{\rm sys}=283\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ for a symmetric SN. Reproducing this value with an asymmetric SN requires a kick velocity of $w\simeq 570\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$ (cf. orange lines). The horizontal grey line marks the local Galactic escape velocity[28] of $v_{\rm esc,\odot}=528\pm 25\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$.

Extended Data Fig. 1 Symmetric supernova. Parameter space for producing a post-SN DNS system with orbital period and eccentricity similar to the current values of PSR J0653+0443 within small error bars ($P=79.1\pm 0.5\;{\rm days}$ and $e=0.992\pm 0.002$) in an (almost) purely symmetric SN ($w\approx 0$, while allowing for mild asymmetry with very small kicks, $w<5\;{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$). Based on simulations of $4\times 10^{7}$ binaries with parameters chosen according to legends in panels C–E. The red arrows indicate precise values for a purely symmetric SN exactly reproducing PSR J0653+0443. Red points in panel F indicate solutions with kick directions along the pre-SN orbital angular-momentum axis.

Extended Data Fig. 2 Asymmetric supernova. Parameter space of purely kinematic solutions producing a post-SN DNS system consistent with the observed PSR J0653+0443 parameters within small error bars ($P=79.1\pm 2.4\;{\rm days}$ and $e=0.992\pm 0.002$) in asymmetric SNe with kicks of $w=0-1000\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$ in isotropic directions. Few systems survive kicks $w>500\;{\rm km\,s}^{-1}$. Based on simulations of $1\times 10^{8}$ binaries with parameters selected according to the legends in panels C–E. The red star in panel A indicates the birth position of the system if it has a true age of $t=1.0\;{\rm Gyr}$. The red points in panel F indicate kick directions along the pre-SN orbital angular-momentum axis. Compare with Extended Data Fig. 5 for “realistic” solutions based on the pulsar spin.

title: Hot off the Stacks: X-rays in Romulus25, Part I - Comparisons to Observations from eRosita
authors: N. Nicole Sanchez, Andrew Benson, Gwen Rudie, Ben Oppenheimer, Hannah Bish, Emily Silich, Phil Hopkins, John ZuHone, Michael Tremmel, Tom Quinn
abstract: Recent observations from the from Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA all-sky survey data have helped to illuminate the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) around galaxies at Milky Way-masses and above. In our study, we explore the hot X-ray emitting (T \textgreater 10$^6$ K) component of the CGM in over 750 galaxies from the Romulus25 cosmological simulation (Tremmel et al. 2017) between 10.0 < log(M$_*/M_{\odot}$) < 11.5. We forward-model soft X-ray [0.5 - 2.0] keV observations of our simulated galaxies using pyXSIM and SIXTE to measure the X-ray surface brightness (SB) profiles of the hot CGM. We then compare the average X-ray surface brightness profiles of six stellar-mass selected sub-samples to compare to the observational results from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. 2024a. Broadly, we find that our stacked SB profiles are too bright compared to observations from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al.(2024a) particularly in the inner CGM. Additionally, we calculate the X-ray luminosity (L$_{\chi}$) of the hot CGM for each galaxy and compare the average L$_{\chi}$ across stellar mass to observations from Zhang et al. (2024b) as well as measurements from the EAGLE, TNG, SIMBA simulations. Across stellar mass, the average L$_{\chi}$ of galaxies from Romulus25 are brighter than observations except at the lower, Milky Way-mass end where we are in relative agreement with both observations and most other simulations. We also consider a zero-metallicity emission model, because Romulus25 does not have metal-line cooling, finding the average L$_{\chi}$ decreases by nearly an order-of-magnitude, which better matches observations particularly in the Milky Way-mass regime.
comments: 13 pages, 6 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal

Galaxies from Rekar sample are shown in pink, with the solid line indicating the median L$_{χ}$ for the simulated galaxies within 0.1 dex M$_{∗}$ bins when we include both Brehmsstrahlung and metal line emission (See Section V.2). The pink shaded region indicates the standard deviation of R25 galaxies’ L$_{χ}$ values. The dashed pink line indicates the mean L$_{χ}$ only considering Brehmsstrahlung emission to account for potentially overabundant hot gas due to a lack of metal cooling in our simulations [For details see Section VII.1]. Purple and dark purple points are X-ray luminosities from observed galaxies with eROSITA [76, as in Figure 2] and yellow points are from [2]. Grey dotted, dashed, and dot dash lines indicate comparable measurements from EAGLE, TNG100, and SIMBA simulation groups. Before correcting for the lack of high temperature metal cooling in Romulus25, the Rekar sample galaxies are at least 0.5 dex higher than observations above a stellar mass of 10$^{11}$ M$_{⊙}$ and we see a much steeper relationship between L$_{χ}$ and M$_{∗}$ than [75]. However, between log(M$_{∗}$) = 10.0 —11.0 M$_{⊙}$, our mean Brehmsstrahlung-only L$_{χ}$ values (dashed pink line) are much closer to matching observed measurements, though our scatter is much wider. Compared to other cosmological simulations, our Brehmsstrahlung-only L$_{χ}$ values sit almost directly between between EAGLE and TNG at the X-ray brightest end and SIMBA at the dimmest in soft X-rays.

title: Resolving the thermal component of stellar feedback with the "anchor-and-refine" scheme in galactic simulations
authors: Chengzhe Li, Hui Li, Wei Cui, Federico Marinacci, Laura Sales, Mark Vogelsberger, Paul Torrey
abstract: (abridged) Stellar feedback regulates galactic baryon cycles, but galaxy-scale simulations often cannot resolve supernova cooling radii. Momentum-based subgrid models can consequently underresolve the hot gas around young stars. We develop an "anchor-and-refine" feedback scheme that anchors a host cell near each star particle, preventing its displacement and preserving a thermal-feedback reservoir. When the cooling radius is resolved, all supernova energy is injected into the host cell as thermal energy; otherwise, the host cell is refined and terminal momentum is deposited into surrounding gas cells. Idealized tests agree with high-resolution simulations, yielding consistent superbubble properties and preserving hot interiors without artificial cooling. In an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy, the scheme captures finer X-ray-emitting structures and a sharply defined, X-ray-bright central mid-plane. It also produces a smoother star formation history than pure hybrid feedback. Hot gas dominates outflow mass loading, with the mass-loading factor plateauing at approximately 0.2 at heights z>1 kpc. Phase decomposition indicates that hot gas sustains a steady, energy-driven wind, whereas cooler outflows decline with height because of radiative cooling and gravitational fallback. These results highlight the role of thermal feedback in driving galactic winds. By preserving hot superbubble interiors and the partition of thermal and kinetic energy, anchor-and-refine improves the treatment of hot gas, star formation, and feedback at limited resolution, supporting future applications to galaxy-scale and cosmological zoom-in simulations.
comments: 11 pages and 8 figs in the main text; A&A in press

title: NORI: a GPU-accelerated code for simulating self-gravitating and self-interacting dark matter
authors: Oliver Zier, Ruediger Pakmor, Xuejian Shen, Rongrong Liu, Lucas Schleuss, Mark Vogelsberger, Lars Hernquist
abstract: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can form cores in dark matter haloes and later drive their gravothermal collapse, raising their central densities far above those of NFW haloes. Simulating this collapse is computationally demanding, requiring increasingly short time-steps and a large particle number to resolve the shrinking core. We present NORI, an $N$-body code that runs on CPUs and GPUs and simulates isolated self-gravitating systems with elastic, isotropic self-interactions using a Monte-Carlo method. To avoid MPI communication in the tree walks, each compute node in CPU mode, and each GPU or group of GPUs in GPU mode, holds a copy of all particles and its own Morton-ordered tree. A fixed evaluation order makes the results bitwise identical on CPUs and GPUs. Applying scattering events sequentially conserves the momentum and energy of each pair to round-off and allows multiple scatterings per particle per step. With global time-steps in both codes, NORI is several times faster on CPUs than our AREPO-2 implementation. One four-A100 GPU node is up to 60 times faster per time-step than AREPO-2 on a 112-core CPU node. For a full core-collapse simulation, where AREPO-2 uses individual time-steps, the speed-up is $\sim 30$ for the central density to reach $10^3$--$10^4$ times the NFW scale density, $\rho_{\rm s}$. We follow a halo with $10^8$ particles within $r_{200}$ to a central density of $10^4\,\rho_{\rm s}$. Within the limit of about $2\times10^9$ particles set by data replication, NORI provides an efficient tool for isolated SIDM simulations, including gravothermal collapse and cluster collisions.

figs.cap: Construction of the tree from the sorted Morton keys, illustrated in two dimensions with twelve particles and at most $K=3$ particles per leaf. Top left: the particles on a grid with 4 bits per coordinate. Interleaving the bits of the grid coordinates $n_{x}$ and $n_{y}$ gives the Morton key $k$ of a particle. Written with one digit per pair of bits, each digit of the key selects one of the four daughter cells at one level. The orange path connects the particles in the order of their keys, and the numbers are their Morton indices $s$. The outlined cells are the leaves A to E, and the grid lines are the cell boundaries of levels 1 to 3. Top right: the sorted particles with their keys. The particles of a leaf at level $\ell$ share the first $\ell$ digits of their keys. The leaves are the same whether the particles are divided into two or into three intervals. Bottom left: the count–scan–write allocation of the nodes for three intervals. Bottom right: the resulting tree, with the position of each node in the node array. The colours mark the rank that creates a leaf or node when the particles are divided into three intervals.

Parallel scattering decisions and ordered update of the velocities. Left: each particle $i$ adjusts its smoothing length $h_{i}$ to enclose the desired neighbour number and tests every neighbour $j$. The trial of the ordered pair $(i,j)$ is accepted if the uniform random number $x_{ij}\in[0,1)$, generated by the Philox generator from $i$, $j$, and the time-step number $n$ (Section 3.6), satisfies $x_{ij}<P(i|j)$. Accepted events are recorded, while all velocities are left unchanged (“frozen”). Middle: the accepted events of all ranks are gathered and sorted by a random 64-bit priority, with $i$ and $j$ breaking ties. This gives one common order $e_{1},\dots,e_{7}$. Right: the ordered update. One rank per replica applies the events serially in this order on the host. Each vertical bar connects the two partners of an event. An open circle marks a particle that already took part in an earlier event of this step. The event then uses its updated velocity. Particle indices are Morton indices.

Right: in the partitioned GPU mode, the GPUs of a compute node share one replica (dashed frame). Each GPU stores one segment and reads particles of other segments through peer-to-peer (P2P) access. title: Extra! Extra! X-ray Emission!: X-rays in Romulus25, Part II - Physical Drivers of X-ray Emission in the CGM
authors: N. Nicole Sanchez, Andrew Benson, Gwen Rudie, Ben Oppenheimer, Hannah Bish, John ZuHone, Michael Tremmel
abstract: Characterizing the hot (T ~ 10$^{6}$ K) circumgalactic medium (CGM) around Milky Way-mass (MW-mass) galaxies is critical to a full understanding of galaxy evolution. In this second paper of the "X-rays in Romulus25" series, we unpack the specific physical processes giving rise to the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas in the halos of galaxies from the Romulus25 (R25) simulation, focusing on L$_{*}$ galaxies. We determine that a strong correlation appears between the mass of hot CGM gas, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, and the X-ray emissivity, $\epsilon_{\chi}$, measured in the first paper of this series, (Sanchez et al. 2026a, submitted). There is also a secondary correlation between M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$ and $\epsilon_{\chi}$ with the average metallicity of the hot CGM gas, $\bar{Z}_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. We use the well-studied PIONEER simulations from Sanchez et al. (2019), a set of zoom-in MW-mass galaxies run with the genetic modification technique of Roth et al. (2016) and the same physics as R25, to interpret these correlations. We determine that the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas is determined by two key processes: 1) the quantity of hot gas mass in the CGM, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, is set by the combined total energy injection of $both$ stellar and AGN feedback, and 2) together the average temperature and metallicity of the hot CGM changes the soft X-ray spectrum of the gas resulting in brighter metal-rich CGM and dimmer metal-poor CGM for the same quantity of M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. These results indicate, for the first time, that metal-rich gas halos may bias X-ray observations of MW-mass galaxies.
comments: 10 pages, 9 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal

title: A double debris disc around a white dwarf sculpted by two planetary bodies
authors: Nicola Pietro Gentile Fusillo, Felipe Lagos-Vilches, Boris T. Gänsicke, Christopher J. Manser, Detlev Koester
abstract: Many planetary systems survive the metamorphosis of their hosts stars into white dwarfs, as demonstrated by the detection of dusty circumstellar discs around these stellar remnants as well as chemical signatures of planetary debris in atmospheres of these stars. A small fraction of these circumstellar discs also contain gas, detected in the form of emission lines from various ionic transitions (most commonly the near-infrared Ca ii triplet). All of the 21 known gas discs exhibit double-peaked line profile characteristic of a rotating flat disc. The mechanism behind the the generation of gas is still debated, but for at least one system it has been linked with the presence of a surviving planetesimal embedded within the dust disc. Here we report the discovery of WD J132800.85-145019.95, a new gas disc system which exhibits quadruple-peaked instead of double-peaked line profiles. These emission lines originate from two separate gaseous rings extending from 0.14 Rsun to 0.34 Rsun and from 0.54 Rsun to 1.93 Rsun. We propose that this structure results from the presence of two distinct planetary bodies within these discs, ranging in size from a few km to the size of Pluto. The detection this stable double-disc presents a new challenge for the current models of debris disc formation and evolution.
comments: 42 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in Nature Astronomy

title: Not so dead after all: young stars in the massive S0 NGC 3115
authors: João P. V. Benedetti, Alexandre Vazdekis, Anna Ferré-Mateu, Elham Eftekhari, Alberto Rodríguez-Ardila, Rogério Riffel
abstract: Context: Massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) are traditionally considered "red-and-dead" based on optical observations. However, ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy can uncover a hidden population of young stars with a sub-one-per cent mass fraction. Aims: We measure the young stellar mass fraction in NGC 3115, a massive isolated lenticular galaxy, to test the ubiquity and spatial distribution of this component beyond previously studied ellipticals. Methods: Using SOAR/Goodman spectra and line-strength fitting, we modelled the star-formation history with a single bulk stellar population plus a young component (constant star-formation over the last 1 Gyr). We used ultranest to derive posterior distributions for age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe], and the young stellar mass fraction. Results: By tracking spatial variations in U-band indices, we found the young stellar mass fraction peaks at $0.69^{+0.09}_{-0.15}\%$ in the centre, dropping to zero beyond 1 kpc. This young component correlates with kinematic structures, dominating in the pressure-supported region. We interpret this as residual central star formation fueled by internal processes, such as recycled stellar material. Alternative UV-bright models (e.g., extreme horizontal branch stars) yielded poorer fits and unphysically high mass fractions. Conclusions: Young stars in old, "red-and-dead" galaxies are more common than expected. Their presence across various ETGs with similar gradients indicates that residual star formation is a ubiquitous feature, offering key constraints on the baryon cycle in these galaxies.

title: Ejected and Rejected: Strong Scatterings in Dense Star Clusters
authors: Adam Distler, Nicholas C. Stone
abstract: Understanding the evolution of collisional stellar systems is key to predicting both the bulk evolution of dense star clusters and also the rates of tidal disruption events, extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar ejections, and other loss cone phenomena. Although a majority of the evolution is dictated by weak, small-angle scatterings, rare close encounters resulting in strong scatterings can sometimes produce qualitatively different outcomes. To systematically determine the astrophysical importance of strong scatterings, we derive the exact differential rate distribution of velocity kicks in isotropic and spherically symmetric distribution functions representing globular and nuclear star clusters, while also deriving the distribution boundaries and approximate rate scalings. We then extend this formalism to derive approximate rates of energy and angular momentum kicks for objects in the nuclear star cluster, and then apply this framework to study (i) ejections and (ii) ``cancellation'' of extreme mass ratio inspirals. We find that ejection rates are complicated in some regimes due to the saturation of the strong kick distribution and the breakdown of the weak limit, likely enhancing the effect of loss cone shielding. We also determine that a sizable fraction of proto-EMRIs will likely be canceled by strong scatterings, highlighting the need for future work to determine to what degree strong scatterings impact the true EMRI rate.
comments: Submitted to ApJ, Comments welcome!

title: The Redshift-Space Cluster-Galaxy Cross-Correlation as a Probe of Gravity on Cosmic Scales
authors: Nicole Marcelina Gountanis, David H. Weinberg, Andrés N. Salcedo, Claire Lamman
abstract: Testing General Relativity (GR) on cosmological scales requires probes that are directly sensitive to gravitational dynamics. We present a Fisher matrix forecast of how well the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) can constrain departures from GR through the cluster infall velocity field, using the redshift-space cluster-galaxy cross-correlation function $\xi^{\rm s}_{\rm cg}(r_p, r_\pi)$ as the primary observable. We construct mock catalogs from the AbacusSummit N-body simulations, using a Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) model for galaxies and a log-normal mass-observable relation for cluster selection. We parameterize departures from GR with a single multiplicative factor $F_{\rm G}$ that rescales halo infall velocities relative to the GR prediction. Marginalizing over the HOD, mass-observable, and cosmological parameters, we find that DESI BGS can constrain $F_{\rm G}$ to $\sigma(F_{\rm G}) = 0.033$ at $z \sim 0.3$. This precision is sufficient to distinguish representative $f(R)$ and Galileon gravity models from GR at $\gtrsim 4\sigma$. The strongest limitation is a degeneracy between $F_{\rm G}$ and the scatter in the cluster mass-observable relation, while the constraint shows no strong degeneracy with any individual HOD parameter. Perfect knowledge of the galaxy-halo connection would improve the constraint to $\sigma(F_{\rm G}) \approx 0.015$, and including the galaxy autocorrelation function in the data vector could recover part of this improvement. The same data vector yields tight constraints on the cosmological parameters, $\sigma(\Omega_m) = 0.010$ and $\sigma(\sigma_8) = 0.010$, only moderately correlated with $F_{\rm G}$. These results demonstrate the potential of DESI BGS cluster-galaxy correlations to test gravity on quasi-linear scales, complementary to existing modified gravity probes and to weak-lensing cluster mass profiles.

title: Revisiting Sub-Neptune Population Synthesis: The Role of Core Luminosity in Boil-off, Photoevaporation, and the Radius Distribution
authors: Yao Tang, Jonathan J. Fortney, Natalie Batalha, Ruth Murray-Clay
abstract: The observed bimodal radius distribution of close-in small planets provides important constraints on their formation and evolution. Two atmospheric escape mechanisms, photoevaporation and core-powered mass loss, have been widely invoked to explain this distribution. In this work, we revisit the physical assumptions underlying these models and investigate the role of core luminosity in driving outflows and shaping the radius distribution. We develop a population synthesis framework based on the SEAMIST evolution model, which self-consistently couples the two mass-loss mechanisms while accounting for envelope metallicity. We find that envelope metallicity strongly affects the resulting radius distribution, with 50-100$\times$ solar metallicity providing a good match to the observed population. Boil-off generally dominates atmospheric mass loss, while photoevaporation typically removes at most 3 wt\% of the envelope mass. We find that core luminosity contributes only $\sim$10-20\% of the thermal energy available for envelope re-equilibration during boil-off, producing an absolute mass-loss enhancement of only $\sim$0.4wt\%. Its effect is larger during photoevaporation, where the longer mass-loss timescale allows core heating to accumulate. Nevertheless, core luminosity has little impact on the long-term planetary radius distribution. These results suggest that core-powered mass loss is better understood as a modification to atmospheric escape through its lower-boundary conditions rather than as a distinct mass-loss mechanism. In our best-fit model, the radiative atmosphere contributes a significant $\sim$20\% of the total optical radius. Consequently, we highlight the need for improved radiative-atmosphere modeling in sub-Neptune evolution models to better understand the observed population distribution.
comments: 17 pages, 8 figures, under review at ApJ Letters

title: Searching for Circumplanetary Dust in the Cavity of the AB Aurigae Disk with ALMA
authors: Lillian Jiang, Brendan P. Bowler, Ya-lin Wu, Yifan Zhou
abstract: The young intermediate-mass star AB Aurigae is surrounded by a transition disk whose cavity contains several proposed protoplanets, including the debated source "AB Aur b" at a projected separation of $\approx 0.6$ arcsec ($\approx 93$ au). To search for circumplanetary material associated with these candidates, we have obtained the most sensitive ($\sim 20$ $\mu$Jy/beam rms) and highest angular resolution ($\sim 30$ mas) ALMA Band 7 (0.88 mm) observations of AB Aur to date. We recover the asymmetric dust ring in the continuum emission peaking at $\sim 0.9$ arcsec ($\sim 140$ au) and compact emission at the stellar position, but detect no point source at the location of AB Aur b or any of the other proposed protoplanet candidates down to a $3\sigma$ limit of $60$ $\mu$Jy. For optically thin emission, this corresponds to a dust mass of $\lesssim 0.0059 M_\oplus$ (for a dust temperature of 40 K), comparable to the circumplanetary disk around PDS 70 c. The $^{12}$CO emission fills the continuum cavity, revealing inner spiral structure and a clear rotation pattern. The gas at the position of AB Aur b is smoothly connected to the ambient disk with no localized excess or obvious kinematic deviation. If any proposed candidates are accreting, their circumplanetary material must have a low dust mass, a small physical size, dust that is optically thick, or a dearth of large mm-emitting grains.
comments: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters

title: Simulation-Informed Dust Masses in Typical $6<z<14$ JWST Galaxies
authors: Jed McKinney, Dhruv T. Zimmerman, Desika Narayanan, Caitlin M. Casey, Julian B. Munoz, Paul Torrey, Hui Li, Federico Marinacci
abstract: Direct detections of dust in typical $z>8$ galaxies remain untenable, despite the presence of dust suggested by rest-frame UV/optical spectro-photometry. Informed by cosmological zoom-in simulations where dust particles evolve on-the-fly, we present a novel method for inferring dust masses in high-redshift galaxies using stellar half-light radii and UV/optical attenuation. Our methods reproduce observed trends at lower redshift, ultimately diverging from Milky Way-based calibration factors by up to $\sim1.5$ dex. We apply this method to observed JWST galaxies from $6<z<14$, and find dust masses in the range $M_{\rm dust}\sim10^3-10^5\,M_\odot$ that are fully consistent with upper limits from ALMA, and suggest an early dust enrichment period by supernovae followed by efficient grain destruction in the hot gas. Future observations may use our tabulated calibration to infer dust masses over a wide range of stellar masses and redshifts.
comments: 8 pages, 5 figures, submitted to ApJL, comments welcome

title: Probing Cosmology with Diffusion Models: Memorization, Generalization, and Parameter Estimation
authors: Jiaming Pan, Nicholas Kern
abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used as surrogates for expensive cosmological simulations, but simple metrics like reconstruction fidelity do not guarantee a surrogate can be trusted for scientific inference. To explore this, we train diffusion models on HI fields from the CAMELS IllustrisTNG simulations and test how three properties change with training-set size: memorization of individual training examples, agreement with one- and two-point statistics (the pixel-value distribution and the power spectrum), and estimation of cosmological parameters from the generated fields. At fixed model size, generative models trained with smaller, less diverse training data produced memorized samples. While this is a well known phenomenon, we show that this leads to miscalibrated parameter densities for cosmological inference tasks. At fixed size, there is a training set size with enough information content to enable a model to generalize, at which point posterior density estimation with neural surrogates can be well-calibrated. We demonstrate that a neural surrogate can therefore pass visual, one-point and power-spectrum convergence tests while still resulting in overconfident parameter estimation in a cosmological inference pipeline. Thus, tests of model generalization should be an additional check for inference pipelines adopting neural surrogates.
comments: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to the Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop 2026

Third and bottom rows: generated mean power spectrum and one-point distribution (512 fields; blue), training data median (dashed), and central 68% (dark grey) and 95% (light grey) training set ranges.

Grey shaded shows the $1\sigma$ confidence interval ground truth of our regression head, while points show recovered parameter values and $1\sigma$ uncertainties at held-out $\Omega_{m}$ values in the test set. title: Early Dark Energy Crowds Out Interacting Dark Energy
authors: William Giarè, Jeremy Sakstein
abstract: We investigate whether interacting dark energy can provide additional relief to the Hubble tension once early dark energy (EDE) is present. Considering a cosmology containing EDE, an independent late-time dark energy fluid with an equation of state fixed at $w\simeq-1$ interacting with cold dark matter, and a cosmological constant, we find that the data strongly drive the model toward the non-interacting limit. The best fit effectively reduces to the standard EDE cosmology, where a non-zero EDE component provides most of the required increase in $H_0$, leaving little statistical gain for the interaction. Although energy transfer from dark matter to dark energy can raise $H_0$ further, this limited gain is rapidly outweighed by the deterioration of the fit to low-redshift observations. In particular, since the CMB tightly constrains the early-time physical matter density, any additional energy transfer requires a lower present-day matter abundance. Such low values are strongly disfavored by Type Ia supernovae. We show that this limitation becomes particularly severe once EDE has already raised $H_0$ and that the same mechanism extends to a broad class of post-recombination interactions. Allowing a dynamical dark energy equation of state of the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder form does not alter our conclusions.
comments: 35 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables

title: Core-collapse universality for inelastic self-interacting dark matter halos
authors: Evan Batteas, Alexander Brisebois, Maheen Hemani, Maximilian Heyne, J. Leo Kim, Lukas Lehmann, Laura Sagunski, Aster Schnell, Sean Tulin
abstract: We study the gravothermal collapse of inelastic dark matter halos with velocity-dependent elastic and dissipative self-interactions. Within the gravothermal fluid framework, we derive the effective cooling rate for dark matter upscattering to an excited state followed by decay back to the ground state, with emitted states carrying off energy from the halo. We solve the gravothermal fluid equations numerically to simulate spherically symmetric halos over the core-growing and collapse phases of their evolution. While halos with purely elastic self-interactions have universal evolution trajectories, inelastic dark matter halos exhibit much more diversity in their evolution. Nevertheless, inelastic halo dynamics contain a hidden parametric universality from which we derive a semi-analytic formula for calculating the halo collapse time for arbitrary velocity-dependent elastic and inelastic cross sections without the need for simulations.
comments: 35 total pages, 7 figures. 24 pages of main text and 11 pages of appendices

title: No Significant Excess in Typical Variability in CLAS+ Changing-Look AGN Candidates in Rubin DP2
authors: Lilianne Nakazono
abstract: Rubin Data Preview 2 (DP2) samples the CLAS+ changing-look AGN (CLAGN) candidates $\sim1,000-9,000$ days after their comparison epochs, so it can test whether these objects retain enhanced short-term optical variability after their spectral transitions. Comparing peak-to-peak amplitude in magnitudes against a photometrically quiescent quasar control, one band at a time, we do not detect a significant median-amplitude excess for any state (turn-on, turn-off, intermediate) in either of two bands, nor a different in the median $\,|\,\Delta \text{mag}\,|\,$ as function of time lag. The $r$-band CLAS+ amplitude distributions are wider than the control's, with the intermediate state formally significant after multiple-comparison correction. This could hint for a high-amplitude subpopulation.

title: The MARTINI platform II. Tracing r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers with long-lived remnants
authors: Eleonora Loffredo, Diego Vescovi, Albino Perego, Federico Maria Guercilena, Sergio Cristallo
abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers are among the primary sites of the rapid neutron-capture (r-)process. In mergers with long-lived remnants, sustained neutrino irradiation raises the electron fraction of the disc wind ejecta, modifying the resulting nucleosynthesis pattern. Yields from numerical-relativity simulations with accurate neutrino transport are needed to quantify the contribution of BNS mergers to the Galactic production of heavy elements and to interpret kilonova spectra. We present and publicly release tracer trajectories and nucleosynthesis yields for eight BNS mergers forming long-lived neutron star remnants, obtained from general-relativistic simulations with M1 neutrino transport, spanning two equations of state (DD2 and SFHo), and a range of total masses and mass ratios. Passive tracer particles following the dynamical and wind ejecta were post-processed with the nuclear reaction network WinNet up to 1 Gyr. The yields and tracer trajectories are available on the MARTINI platform. At 1 day, the production of light and first-peak elements (He, Ni, Sr, and Y) is similar across models and is primarily enhanced by the neutrino-irradiated disc wind. The yields of heavy nuclei vary by more than one order of magnitude, with unequal-mass binaries producing the largest amounts owing to their more neutron-rich ejecta. Our He yields, particularly in the wind, exceed those of recent studies based on an M0 neutrino scheme, consistent with the stronger neutrino irradiation resulting from an M1 scheme. At 1 Gyr, all models reproduce the second and third solar r-process peaks, but differ in the first peak, the lanthanide region, the mass range between the first and second peaks, and the trans-lead region, reflecting the electron fraction distribution of the ejecta and the dynamical and wind contributions. Two equal-mass models provide a close match to the solar pattern.
comments: 20 pages, 15 figures

title: Considering Numerical Relativity Surrogate Models for AGN Channel Merger Dynamics
authors: Shawn Ray, Keefe Mitman, Vera Delfavero, Emily McPike, Jake Postiglione, Harrison E. Cook, Kaila Nathaniel, Nicolas Posner, Barry McKernan, K.E. Saavik Ford, Richard O'Shaughnessy
abstract: Binary black hole mergers (BBH) are currently observed by the gravitational-wave detectors LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA (LVK). A fraction of these mergers are likely to originate in active galactic nuclei (AGN), but the details of the dynamical processes driving AGN channel mergers remain poorly understood. Monte Carlo For AGN Channel Testing and Simulation (McFACTS) is an open-source, public software used to simulate AGN channel BBH formation and evolution with configurable options for exploring various AGN and Nuclear Star Cluster (NSC) parameter options. Within McFACTS, BBH mergers evolve through gas drag and dynamical interactions, ignoring relativistic effects which can influence merger remnant properties. Here we demonstrate in McFACTS the effect of handing off inspiralling BBH to a numerical relativity (NR) surrogate model, which more accurately predicts the masses, spins, and kick velocities of merger remnants. Compared to a simple analytic approach to calculating merger and remnant properties the NR surrogate model is significantly more accurate at predicting remnant spins, which improve $\chi_{eff}$ and $\chi_{p}$ calculations, and recoil kicks, parameters especially important for higher generation BBH mergers. Our findings show the NR surrogate significantly changes distributions of remnant spins and kick velocities, as well as showing that alternative methods should be used cautiously in future studies. We also outline some simple models which are computationally efficient and can reproduce much of the NR surrogate model results.

title: Validating an X-ray-based method for identifying Fermi blazars
authors: J. L. Weiss, E. J. Marchesini, I. Andruchow, N. Masetti
abstract: Context. Blazars are the main population of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) detected in gamma rays by Fermi. However, around 34% of Fermi sources remain unidentified, partly due to their large positional uncertainties, motivating multiwavelength methods to identify possible counterparts. Aims. We evaluate a method proposed to identify BL Lacertae (BL Lac) candidates among unidentified Fermi sources based on their X-ray properties, using Swift-XRT observations. Methods. We examined published optical spectra for an initial sample of 148 X-ray-selected candidates. We found 71 sources with spectra spatially consistent with the proposed associations and reassessed their classifications using standard blazar criteria. We then compared these classifications with the method's initial predictions. Results. Of the 71 proposed counterparts, 80.28% are classified as BL Lac objects and 87.32% as possible gamma-ray-emitting AGNs, supporting the effectiveness of the X-ray-based selection. We also identify four Seyfert galaxies, suggesting that the method is sensitive to this class despite its rarity among gamma-ray emitters. Conclusions. Our results show that X-ray observations are effective for selecting BL Lac candidates among unidentified Fermi sources and support future spectroscopic follow-up campaigns. The high fraction of BL Lacs and AGNs suggests that blazars may account for a substantial part of the unidentified gamma-ray population. The Seyfert identifications also raise questions about the origin of high-energy emission in AGNs not typically associated with relativistic jets, highlighting the need for further multiwavelength observations.

title: Machine learning applications in the heliosphere
authors: Vishal Upendran, Banafsheh Ferdousi
abstract: Space weather is the study of the near-Earth impact of the processes on the Sun. In a this era of technology, space weather emerges as a crucial area of study wherein the state of the near-Earth conditions need to be modeled and forecasted. Crucially, the advent of machine learning provides us with opportunities to study this subject in a rather comprehensive manner. In this chapter, we treat the the processes arising from Sun to the impact on the ground as a set of coupled systems, which can be studied in isolation or in a coupled manner. We define these individual systems in terms of their state vector $\vec{S}$, which provides us with an opportunity to define the physical variables determining the system. This also allows us to consider the systems in terms of their observables, obtained through the action of operators as $\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$. In such a formalism, the machine learning algorithms serve as {\it learned operators}, defined generally as inference ($\mathcal{I}$), propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and emulation ($\mathcal{E}$). Through such a formalism, we present how machine learning helps advance our understanding of the physical systems under study, while also accelerating the development of operational models for space weather forecasting.
comments: Review chapter submitted to the book Machine Learning Techniques for Astrophysics and Cosmology by Spring Singapore

title: Simulating and Characterizing Non-Gaussian Small-Scale Polarized Emission
authors: Mark A. Bishop, Brandon S. Hensley, Krzysztof M. Gorski, Charles Lawrence, Graça Rocha
abstract: Galactic foregrounds present a major challenge for cosmic microwave background (CMB) cosmology as their amplitudes exceed the target primordial $B$-mode signal. While small-scale interstellar medium (ISM) emission is expected to be highly complex, current foreground simulations cannot reproduce the filamentary, non-Gaussian features of ISM structure in a stochastic way. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for generating stochastic small-scale foreground emission, using polarized synchrotron observations as an example use case. This method is capable of producing many independent realizations that additionally inherit morphological information from large angular scales. The underlying structural complexity incorporates anisotropic, multifractal, and advected non-Gaussian features that are tunable with a small number of parameters that carry physical interpretations. Because standard power spectra do not describe the complex phase coherence required for the structural complexity, we evaluate the synthetic fields using higher-order statistics, demonstrating that the Minkowski functionals and structure functions partially capture varying degrees of non-Gaussianity. This work lays the necessary foundation for new foreground simulation suites with stochastic realizations of possible non-Gaussian structure.
comments: 25 pages, 19 figures, submitted to APJ

title: Probabilistic Stellar Mass and Radius Estimation with Bayesian Hierarchical Stacking
authors: Maxence Lamirel, Andrés Moya, Roberto J. López-Sastre, Luis Manuel Sarro
abstract: Accurate stellar parameters are essential for the characterisation of exoplanets, yet most host stars lack direct measurements of mass and radius. We aim to predict stellar masses and radii from commonly available observables and to quantify uncertainties and systematic effects in a way that is consistent with stellar observations. By not relying on a single model, we aim to obtain more robust predictive distributions and reduce sensitivity to model misspecification and outliers. We develop a Bayesian machine-learning framework that combines three probabilistic models through Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS): a Bayesian additive regression tree model, a two-process heteroscedastic sparse Gaussian process, and a hierarchical Bayesian neural network. The method propagates measurement uncertainties, accounts for correlations among inputs, and aggregates model variance into final predictive distributions. On a held-out test set the method attains a mean absolute relative difference (MARD) of 3.5% for mass and 2.1% for radius, improving on empirical-relation-based methods and standard machine-learning baselines. For 44 Kepler LEGACY stars, the BHS masses differ from estimates obtained with the BAyesian STellar Algorithm (BASTA) by a MARD of 4.8%, compared with 8.5% between the empirical relations and BASTA. Applied to about 2400 exoplanet host stars, the predictions differ from literature values by a MARD of 2.7% in both mass and radius. Residual analysis reveals mild underestimation for cool dwarfs, consistent with sparse training coverage, and positive offsets near the main-sequence turn-off that may reflect priors in isochrone-based catalogues. Internal consistency with g = GM/R^2 is greater for the BHS predictions, with a scatter in Delta log g lower by a factor of three than that of the literature values.

title: The Carousel Lens III: Joint lens convergence and source kinematic modeling
authors: William Sheu, Xiaosheng Huang, Tania M. Barone, Fuyan Bian, Aleksandar Cikota, Karl Glazebrook, Tesla Jeltema, Evan Odell, Jackson H. O'Donnell, Linus Upson, Felipe Urcelay, Sean Xu
abstract: We introduce a new, independent modeling component to the Carousel Lens series by exploiting the spatially-resolved kinematics contained within the lensed arcs, which so far has remained rather underexplored in strong-lensing analyses. We present an end-to-end forward-modeling framework that reconstructs an integral-field spectroscopic datacube from a parameterization of the lens convergence profile together with the line-of-sight velocity, velocity dispersion, and surface brightness profiles of the unlensed source. The kinematic structure of the source acts as an additional set of ray-traceable markers distributed across every lensed image, inaccessible from imaging data alone. Furthermore, by generating an [OII] emission-line datacube, we isolate a single source redshift and remove lens and line-of-sight light contamination. We apply this framework to deep VLT/MUSE observations of the Carousel Lens, modeling the [OII] emission of the quadruply-imaged star-forming galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$ that anchors the system's cosmography constraints. We measure an Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E} = 12.816''^{+0.005}_{-0.007}$ and a logarithmic slope $\gamma = 1.412^{+0.002}_{-0.002}$, tightening the statistical uncertainties on both by roughly a factor of $2-2.5$ relative to the corresponding flat emission-line map model. We find that the source galaxy exhibits a strong rotation, lies confidently along the star-forming main sequence, and has an inferred central black hole mass of $\log M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot} = 7.89 \pm 0.51$. These results establish datacube-level forward modeling as a practical and independent route to traditional image-based lens models in the current systematics-limited regime, and one that extends naturally to this system's other lensed sources and to other lens systems.

title: Search for Eccentric Neutron Star-Black Hole Binaries in Advanced LIGO's Fourth Observing Run using Effective-One-Body Waveforms
authors: Aleyna Akyüz, Keisi Kacanja, Rahul Dhurkunde, Alexander H. Nitz
abstract: The observation of orbital eccentricity in compact binary coalescences would provide a direct signature of dynamical formation environments. Previous matched-filter searches for eccentric neutron star-black hole (NSBH) binaries have been severely limited by computational constraints, necessitating the use of simplified waveform models that capture secular dephasing but omit apsidal precession and inter-orbit harmonics. Including these physical features increases the sensitive search volume for systems with $0.2 \le e_{20} \le 0.28$ by $\sim 25\%$ to $30\%$. We present a rapid matched-filter search methodology that makes the direct use of time-domain effective-one-body waveforms computationally feasible. By multibanding and high-frequency ratio-filtering, our pipeline achieves a $\sim 20\times$ reduction in computational cost. This allows a bank of 88.6 million effective-one-body templates, fifteen times larger than prior eccentric analyses, to search O4a and O4b Advanced LIGO data. We recover the known low-mass mergers GW230518_125908 and GW230529_181500 with parameters consistent with zero eccentricity. Finding no new gravitational-wave events with orbital eccentricity ($e_{20} \ge 0.05$), we place $90\%$ credible upper limits on the local merger rate density of eccentric NSBH systems across the search space of $\mathcal{R}_{90\%} \le 7.5\text{-}57\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, up to a factor of $\sim 4$ improvement over previous observational bounds. At the parameters of GW200105_162426, this non-detection establishes an upper limit of $\mathcal{R}_{90\%} \le 12.1\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$. Alternatively, if GW200105_162426 is treated as an eccentric detection, the lack of subsequent detections in O4 updates the inferred local merger rate density of this population to $\mathcal{R} = 6.6^{+6.3}_{-3.8}\ \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}\ \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$.

title: Phase-resolved X-ray spectroscopy of the Vela pulsar with NICER observations
authors: E. Zubieta, F. García, S. del Palacio, J. A. Combi, F. A. Fogantini
abstract: PSR J0835-4510 (a.k.a. the Vela pulsar) is the best studied pulsar in the Southern hemisphere given its high radio brightness and large glitch activity. However, its X-ray brightness is comparatively lower, making the study of its X-ray profile difficult. We aim to investigate the X-ray emission of the Vela pulsar coming from the surface of the neutron star to infer the properties of its hotspots and assess whether they share a common spectral shape. We also aim to prove whether the 2021 glitch affected the hotspots. We used ephemeris obtained from high-cadence radio observations with the radio telescopes of the Argentine Institute of Radio Astronomy to combine all the NICER observations of the Vela pulsar after its 2019 glitch and before its 2024 glitch. We obtained a folded pulse profile for three different energy ranges and subsequently studied their phase-resolved energy spectra. We additionally analyzed a Chandra observation to quantify the pulsar's contribution to the total soft X-ray emission detected by NICER, which cannot spatially resolve the pulsar from the surrounding pulsar wind nebula (PWN). The pulsar contribution to the total observed emission represents less than 40-45% of the flux below 0.9 keV, dropping to 3-4% in the 0.9-2.0 keV range and further down to ~2% above 2 keV, where the PWN fully dominates. We find that the X-ray folded profile of the Vela pulsar was not measurably perturbed by the 2021 glitch. We studied separately seven regions of the pulse profile. We found that all of them are well modeled by one or two blackbodies. The temperatures of these hotspots are between $0.79(7) \times 10^{6}$ K $\leq T \leq 4.8^{+0.8}_{-0.6} \times 10^{6}$ K, while their sizes vary between $0.048^{+0.016}_{-0.009}$ km $\leq R \leq 3.9^{+0.9}_{-0.6}$ km, and their luminosities between $5\times10^{30}$ erg/s $\lesssim L < 1\times10^{32}$ erg/s.
comments: 10 pages, 9 Figures, 5 Tables

title: Focal plane modal estimation of high-order wavefront drifts on coronagraphic testbeds
authors: Saikrishna Manojkumar, Susan F. Redmond, Leonid Pogorelyuk, Christine L. Page, Garreth Ruane, Niyati Desai, Kerri Cahoy
abstract: The upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) requires precise wavefront stability over long observation periods to directly image Exo-Earths, which are 10 orders of magnitude dimmer than their host star. Dark zone maintenance (DZM) has been proposed as a focal plane high-order wavefront sensing and control (HOWFSC) strategy to mitigate thermal and mechanical instabilities that cause slow-evolving high-order wavefront drifts, which ultimately degrade contrast. Here we present a modal dark zone maintenance (MDZM) algorithm that uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate the drifting wavefront modes in the basis of the deformable mirror (DM) actuators used for control. The estimator derives information across the entire focal plane from probe-pair images, addressing deficiencies of DZM, and directly obtains a DM command, eliminating the need for Electric Field Conjugation (EFC) and its regularization parameter. MDZM has been demonstrated in simulation and in hardware on the Decadal Survey Testbed (DST) at NASA JPL. These experiments have maintained a normalized intensity (NI) of $\sim 3 \times 10^{-10}$ for over 36 hours, and have reduced the gap to the photon-derived theoretical bounds compared to DZM. MDZM also provides an estimate of naturally occurring drift on the testbed, offering potential system identification capabilities. To evaluate the robustness of MDZM, a parameter scan is conducted on DST, spanning exposure times and drift rates. Additionally, realistic observing scenarios for HWO will involve broadband images with a 20% bandwidth, rather than the 2.5% narrowband images previously used in MDZM testbed demonstrations. Therefore, we tested MDZM in simulation using broadband sensing images with a 10% bandwidth, using the FALCO software package with a model based on DST, and compared its performance against MDZM runs using narrowband images.

title: Tidal shells as clocks of galaxy mergers and tests of cosmological models
authors: Ivana Ebrová, Michal Bílek, Elisabeth Sola, Pierre-Alain Duc, Ana Lalović
abstract: Stellar shells-concentric arc-like tidal features formed in galaxy mergers-provide a valuable record of recent galaxy assembly histories encoding both the merger event and the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. We compare shell systems in observations and cosmological simulations from two complementary perspectives. First, we show that simulations predict a substantial population of very large (>100kpc) shells that are rarely observed, revealing a potentially important discrepancy between simulations and reality. Because the scales of observed and simulated shell systems differ significantly, we focus on a comparison of merger histories. Using a shell-identification method, we estimate merger times for a sample of nearby massive prolate rotators and compare them with merger histories derived from cosmological simulations. We also present ongoing efforts to expand the sample of deeply imaged prolate rotators using observations from the Milankovic telescope, paving the way for future studies based on larger observational samples.

title: Evolutionary Demographics of Molecular Ice Mantles in Young Stars with SPHEREx
authors: J. Serna, S. P. Matt, M. McClure, M. Kounkel, C. G. Roman-Zuñiga
abstract: Molecular ices are a primary reservoir of volatile C, O, and N in star-forming environments, tracing the chemical pathway from molecular clouds to planet-forming disks. SPHEREx provides contiguous 0.75--5~$\mu$m all-sky spectrophotometry for vastly larger samples than are accessible to JWST, enabling population-scale ice demographics for the first time. We present a search for ice signatures in SPHEREx spectra of 20{,}292 young stellar objects (age $<20$~Myr) drawn from the Gaia-based kinematic catalog of Kounkel \& Covey 2019. Using laboratory templates for the spectral signatures of H$_2$O (3.05~$\mu$m), CO$_2$ (4.27~$\mu$m), and CO (4.67~$\mu$m), we identify 746 H$_2$O ice candidates, including 131 high-confidence H$_2$O+CO$_2$ detections and 22 with additional corroborating CO absorption. When binning by age, we find that the H$_2$O$+$CO$_2$ detection rate declines by an order of magnitude between $\lesssim$3~Myr and $\sim$5~Myr, suggesting a chemical or physical evolutionary trend. Candidates concentrate toward high-extinction sightlines ($A_G \gtrsim 2.5$~mag) and embedded SED morphologies, consistent with the idea of envelope dispersal and photodesorption depleting detectable ice mantles within the first few million years of pre-main-sequence evolution. This catalog provides a homogeneous demographic baseline and a prioritized target list for JWST follow-up.
comments: 25 pages, 8 Figures, 6 Tables. Manuscript submitted to The Astrophysical Journal

title: Cosmic rays in galaxy halos I: the circumgalactic transport rate and a dynamically significant cosmic-ray reservoir
authors: Roland M. Crocker, Mark R. Krumholz
abstract: Fermi-LAT observations imply that most of the cosmic rays (CRs) produced in normal star-forming galaxies escape from the discs where they are accelerated into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), but the subsequent evolution of those escaping CRs is unclear. Here we construct a simple semi-analytic model for their transport and loss, which we constrain by confronting the model with a series of observations: limits on CR energy densities in the outer Milky Way from Fermi-LAT, the isotropic gamma-ray background (IGRB), stacked CGM X-ray emission from eROSITA, and the requirement that the accumulated pressure of CRs in galaxy CGMs not be so large as to render them unstable. We show that these constraints can be jointly satisfied in only two scenarios: one where CRs diffuse quickly through the CGM and freely escape beyond it into the IGM, and another where the CR diffusion time out of halos is of order the Hubble time. In the latter scenario CRs accelerated by star formation naturally explain both the IGRB and the heat input required to maintain the temperature of the CGM against X-ray cooling, and their relatively slow transport means that roughly half of the CR energy injected into the CGM of an $L_\star$ halo over its star-formation history remains there at $z \simeq 0$. This makes CR pressure dynamically significant, and also means that a non-negligible part of the IGRB is produced by CRs in the Milky Way's own halo. We argue that this latter scenario is the more likely one, as it avoids the need to posit a second source for the IGRB that is coincidentally very close in both power and spectral shape to the contribution from star-forming discs.
comments: 18 pages of main text with 10 figures; 2 appendices. Constructive community feedback welcomed in advance of submission
