title: Shock detection in meshless finite mass hydrodynamic schemes
authors: Ludwig M. Böss, Frederik Groth, Klaus Dolag, Damiano Caprioli
abstract: Shocks are prevalent in a multitude of astrophysical plasmas. They are essential in the dissipation of gravitational potential energy during structure formation, where they channel it into heat, turbulence, magnetic fields, and particle acceleration. Accurately capturing shocks in simulations of cosmological structure formation is a considerable challenge, due to the complexity of overlapping and colliding shocks, embedded in a medium experiencing complex shear flows. Fully Lagrangian hydrodynamical methods have historically been inferior in this regard compared to Eulerian or pseudo-Lagrangian methods. This work aims to remedy this discrepancy. We present the first efforts to implement a shockfinder algorithm with shock surface reconstruction for meshless finite mass (MFM) hydrodynamic schemes. We show its accuracy compared to analytic predictions and a legacy smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH)- based shock-finding method. We apply this new shock-finding method to simulations of cosmic structure formation to obtain improved predictions for shock energy dissipation and cosmic ray (CR) acceleration.
comments: 14 pages, 11 figures, comments welcome

title: Towards constraining cosmology with HI--galaxy cross-correlations from MeerKLASS
authors: G. Autieri, M. Spinelli, Z. Chen, M. Viel, M. Barberi-Squarotti, P. Bull, S. Camera, I. P. Carucci, S. Cunnington, J. Fonseca, K. Grainge, M. O. Irfan, Y. Li, A. Pourtsidou, M. G. Santos, J. Wang, L. Wolz
abstract: We present an inference of cosmological parameters from the cross-correlation power spectrum between the MeerKLASS 2019 L-band HI intensity maps and the overlapping WiggleZ galaxies at $z \simeq 0.43$. The analysis is intended as a proof of concept to verify that the full pipeline, from the foreground cleaning of the maps to the likelihood analysis, can be applied end-to-end to real data and can return results consistent with the concordance cosmology. The model of the observed power spectrum includes observational effects that are relevant to a single-dish experiment. In the most optimistic scenario in which we hold the astrophysical nuisance parameters fixed, we obtain $H_0 = 65.3^{+5.8}_{-10}\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ and $\Omega_{\text{m}} = 0.44^{+0.12}_{-0.30}$ at the 68% confidence level. We find that sampling the HI amplitude with an informative prior retains most of the constraining power and changes these results by less than 1 sigma. Moreover, using synthetic data, we show that neglecting the observational effects in the model biases the inferred parameters by up to 2.5 sigma and also underestimates their uncertainties. Finally, we show that varying the number of foreground modes removed and the range of scales included changes the inferred parameters by less than 0.5 sigma. These results demonstrate the robustness of our pipeline in modelling HI intensity mapping data, and set the foundation for future cosmological inference with intensity mapping using MeerKLASS and SKAO.

title: Probing the local primordial non-Gaussianity with clustering of FRB dispersion measure and galaxies
authors: Indranil Das, Gilbert Holder
abstract: We forecast the sensitivity of a joint fast radio burst (FRB) and galaxy survey to local primordial non-Gaussianity using the full $3\times2$-point statistic: the angular dispersion-measure (DM) auto-spectrum, the DM-galaxy cross-spectrum, and the galaxy auto-spectrum. Local primordial non-Gaussianity imprints a scale-dependent bias on both the free-electron field probed by FRB dispersion measures and the galaxy field. Hence, all three spectra carry information on the local non-Gaussianity amplitude $f_{\rm NL}$. Adopting a DESI-like luminous-red-galaxy sample and an FRB population over 35% of the sky, we forecast $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 5$ for both $N_{\rm FRB} = 10^4$ and $10^5$ at fixed Planck 2018 cosmology, marginalised over three astrophysical bias parameters $(b_e^0, z_{\rm fb}, b_g^{\rm amp})$. The $f_{\rm NL}$ constraint is robust to marginalising over the six $\Lambda$CDM parameters $(\omega_b, \omega_{\rm cdm}, h, A_s, n_s, \tau)$ with Planck priors. At these sample sizes, the galaxy auto-spectrum sets the constraint, while the DM sector's contribution grows with the burst count and becomes decisive for the larger samples anticipated in the SKA era, reaching $\sigma(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 2$ at $10^7$ bursts.

title: lenscape: Fast, High-resolution $Δχ^2$ Maps of Microlensing Events
authors: Michael Hippke
abstract: Planetary microlensing analyses rely on $\Delta\chi^2$ maps across the binary-lens separation $s$ and mass ratio $q$ to locate degenerate solutions and bound parameter uncertainties. Because every grid point requires a full light-curve optimization with finite-source magnifications, constructing these maps is often the primary computational bottleneck in event modeling. Here I present lenscape, an open-source Python package that accelerates $\Delta\chi^2$ mapping and suppresses local-minimum artifacts through multi-stage neighbor propagation and adaptive contour refinement. Applied to the planetary event MOA-2022-BLG-091, lenscape reproduces the published $50\times50$ map in 14 minutes and generates a $400\times400$ map in under two hours on a desktop computer.
comments: Accepted for publication in AAS journals; 1 figure; code available at this https URL

Panels (b) and (d) display the continuous $\Delta\chi^{2}$ surfaces computed with lenscape at $400\times 400$ resolution. Top row (a, b): $(\log s,\log q)$ plane. Bottom row (c, d): trajectory angle $\alpha$ versus $\log s$, with $\chi^{2}$ profiled over all remaining parameters (including $q$) at each grid point.

title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger
authors: Christian Partmann, Rachel S. Somerville, Michaela Hirschmann, Antti Rantala, Natalia Lahén
abstract: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.
comments: 23 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!

title: ARRAKIHS: The observability of tidally stripped satellites in a Milky Way-like halo
authors: Abram Pérez-Herrero, Y. Revaz, S. Roca-Fàbrega, S. T. Nagesh, J. Preston, D. Erkal, D. Herranz Muñoz, O. Agertz, M. Akhlaghi, R. Bieri, A. Camazón-Pinilla, J. Cenarro, A. P. Cooper, H. Domínguez Sánchez, A. Fattahi, R. Feldmann, A. Font, M. A. Gómez-Flechoso, E. Gaztañaga, M. Güdel, R. Guzmán, E. Illés, R. Infante-Sainz, C. Kintziger, A. Marín-Franch, D. Martínez-Delgado, B. Moore, K. Nagamine, P. Papaderos, P. Renard Guiral, A. H. Riley, R. Rodríguez-Cardoso, S. Serrano, S. Shen, E. Sola, F. Torradeflot, M. Wiesmann
abstract: Deep imaging surveys are revealing increasing numbers of low surface brightness stellar streams around Milky Way-like galaxies. These streams trace the orbital evolution and internal structure of their disrupted dwarf galaxy progenitors. We investigate the evolution and observability of tidal features from dwarf galaxies consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM framework and Local Group observations. We performed high-resolution $N$-body simulations of dwarf galaxies orbiting in a static Milky Way-like potential comprising a disc, bulge, and dark matter halo. Each dwarf comprised a Plummer stellar distribution embedded in a cuspy or cored generalised Navarro--Frenk--White dark matter halo. Idealised integrated surface brightness maps were constructed every 0.5 Gyr over 10 Gyr, and detectability was quantified through the projected area of stellar light brighter than limiting surface brightnesses, $\mu_{\rm lim}=29$--$32$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, chosen to span depths relevant to ARRAKIHS, LSST, and Euclid. The detectability of tidal features depends most strongly on progenitor stellar mass, orbital configuration, parameterised by the eccentricity proxy $e_0$, and evolutionary stage. Across this range, extended tidal debris is predominantly recovered for initially more radial configurations, mainly those with $e_0 \gtrsim 0.75$. In the simulated grid, detectable area is dominated by $M_\star=10^8$--$10^9 M_\odot$ progenitors, whereas $M_\star=10^6$--$10^7 M_\odot$ systems can undergo stripping without detectable debris. The detectable area evolves non-monotonically with time, reflecting the competition between stream formation, phase mixing, and the fading of diffuse debris below the adopted surface brightness limits. Cuspy and cored progenitors show similar evolution of the detectable area, with differences smaller than the scatter induced by orbital diversity.
comments: 16 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)

title: Rotation and outburst-like brightenings in ZZ Ceti stars observed by TESS
authors: Zs. Bognár, Á. Sódor
abstract: Context. Pulsating white dwarfs, such as ZZ Ceti stars, allow for the study of white dwarf rotation through rotationally split pulsation modes. Space-based photometry has also revealed outbursts in some cool ZZ Ceti stars. Aims. We extend the search for rotationally split pulsation multiplets and outburst-like brightenings among known ZZ Ceti stars observed by TESS. We check whether the TESS data add new evidence for a connection between outburst activity and stellar rotation. Methods. We analysed 120 s and 20 s cadence TESS light curves available up to Sector 96. After light curve correction and quality filtering, we performed iterative frequency analysis. Candidate rotationally split multiplets were identified automatically and visually validated. Outburst candidates were selected from smoothed flux excursions, followed by light curve inspection and pixel-level TESS diagnostics. Results. We identify 11 ZZ Ceti stars with accepted triplet candidates and derive rotation periods of about 8-94 h; three triplet detections are reported here for the first time. The targets are broadly consistent with the dispersion of rotation periods found in previous studies. The time-domain search produced 19 outburst-like events in 11 stars after light curve inspection. Pixel-level diagnostics indicate that most are likely caused by foreground asteroid contamination. We identify three stars (TIC 219442838, TIC 307908863, and TIC 630426257) as candidate stellar outbursters. None belong to the accepted triplet-rotation sample.
comments: 18 pages, 11 figures, 1 table available on CDS; accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: The extragalactic science of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey II: Discovery of a galaxy cluster at z = 0.089 behind the Galactic plane
authors: E. O. Schmidt, C. Valotto, C. Villalon, L. D. Baravalle, J. L. Nilo-Castellón, M. V. Alonso, M. Soto, M. Gómez, D. Minniti, W. Weidmann, D. Mast, C. Obasi, D. Alvarez Rocha, S. Federle, R. K. Saito, V. D. Ivanov, M. G. Navarro, Z. Guo, A. Pichel, I. Petralia, V. Fermiano, A. Luna, M. Lad, J. Osses, R. Pignata, V. Valdivia Rojas, P. Marchant Cortes, E. G. Rivera, G. Ferrero, N. Masetti, J. Borissova, J. G. Fernández-Trincado, C. Cáceres, F. Nogueras-Lara, D. Galdeano, F. Fortuni
abstract: The Zone of Avoidance (ZoA) continues to represent the most significant incompleteness in the extragalactic census of the Local Universe. It is evident that photometric surveys alone are insufficient to establish whether the galaxy overdensities detected therein are physical systems or projections along the line of sight. We present the first spectroscopic results of the extragalactic science area of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, demonstrating how near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy can reveal and dynamically characterise galaxy clusters hidden by the Milky Way. A photometric overdensity of 19 galaxy candidates was identified in the VVV NIRGC III catalogue, centred at $(l,b)=(274.05^\circ,+2.85^\circ)$ with a mean interstellar extinction of $A_{K_s}=0.2$ mag; 16 of these candidates were observed with VLT/KMOS in the $HK$ grating and yielded spectra with reliable cross-correlation radial velocities. A total of 14 galaxies form a compact structure with a mean redshift of $\langle z \rangle = 0.089 \pm 0.001$, which corresponds to a mean radial velocity $\langle cz \rangle = 26660 \pm 170$ km/s, while two are foreground galaxies. The rest-frame line-of-sight velocity dispersion is $\sigma_v = 560^{+110}_{-120}$ km/s, implying an indicative dynamical mass of $M_{200} = 1.9^{+0.7}_{-1.1} \times 10^{14} M_\odot$ (based on members within the cluster core $\sim 0.4 r_{200}$) and placing the system in the poor-cluster regime. Of these 14 cluster members, 13 also lie within the $2\sigma$ scatter of the fitted near-IR red sequence. The other two galaxies are foreground objects that lie outside this range.

title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation
authors: Asha Abd, Karl Glazebrook, Colin Jacobs
abstract: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.
comments: 22 pages, 17 figures. Submitted to MNRAS

title: The Bochum Survey of the Southern Galactic Disk: IV. Multi-Band Photometry
authors: Julia Blex, Dominik J. Bomans, Kerstin Weis, Markus Demleitner, Moritz Hackstein, Anna Franckowiak, Michael Ramolla, Christian Westhues, Christofer Fein, Rolf Chini
abstract: The Southern Galactic Disk Survey (GDS) monitored a mosaic of 268 fields along a $6^\circ$-wide stripe in the southern galactic disk from September 2010 to September 2019. These fields were observed between 21 and 407 times simultaneously in $r'$ ($8\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim r' \lesssim 18\,\mathrm{mag}$) and $i'$ ($7\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim i' \lesssim 17\,\mathrm{mag}$), supplemented by between 2 and 147 observations in each of the bands $U$, $B$, $V$, and $z'$. Here we present the matched multi-band catalogue, which integrates photometry and light curve data from all bands, containing photometry for almost 21.7 million Gaia DR3 sources, of which $113\,449$ are identified as variables. We give an overview of the survey's variable content with respect to its main characteristics and known variability type classifications. The comparison with the cross-match catalogue of Gaia DR3 sources with variables from the literature compiled by Gavras et al. (2023) and the International Variable Star Index (VSX) indicates that approximately $40\,\%$ of the variable sources remain unclassified in terms of variability type. Light curves for all of these sources are contained in the GDS data catalogues, available via the German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO), and can contribute to their classification.

title: Environmental Quenching of Satellite Galaxies out to z~0.4 with GAMA and DEVILS
authors: Megan Oxland, Matías Bravo, Laura Parker, Luke Davies, Sabine Bellstedt
abstract: While numerous studies have shown that satellite galaxies experience declining star formation rates after infall, direct comparisons across different surveys and redshifts are complicated by varying sample selections, environmental metrics, and techniques used to derive galaxy properties. In this work, we select satellite galaxies from the highly complete Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey and the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) to investigate environmental quenching out to z~0.4. These surveys derive galaxy properties and environments in a consistent manner, minimizing systematic biases and enabling a robust comparison across redshift. Using projected phase space as a proxy for infall time, we quantify the evolution of the quenched fraction and trace how satellites evolve relative to the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). We find consistent trends between GAMA and DEVILS, with satellites exhibiting a steady decline in star formation relative to the SFMS at a rate of ~0.14 dex/Gyr following infall. Extending this analysis to include visual morphology, we find similar declining trends for both early- and late-type systems. Overall, we find no significant redshift evolution between GAMA and DEVILS, indicating that group and cluster environments have a comparable impact on the star formation activity of satellite galaxies over the past ~4.5 Gyr.
comments: 22 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ

title: SuperCrude EoS: A Simple, Analytical, and Reasonably Accurate Equation of State for Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
authors: Paul C. Duffell, Dillon Hasenour
abstract: We present SuperCrude, a vastly simplified astrophysical equation of state that captures the most important physics needed for explosive astrophysics, but using compact, physically-motivated analytical approximations rather than precise interpolated data tables. We present a number of code tests demonstrating the performance of SuperCrude in a wide range of parameter space. In large regions of parameter space, SuperCrude is precisely accurate to within the accuracy level of helmeos. For some regions (especially where degeneracy, gas, and radiation are comparable) SuperCrude has errors in its effective adiabatic index on the order of a few percent. The solver's estimate of the temperature is less accurate, on the order of tens of percent. Because the solver is analytic, SuperCrude is designed in such a way to guarantee exact thermodynamic consistency. We incorporate SuperCrude into some hydrodynamic and astrophysical test problems, including the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf star. When coupled with a stiff nuclear network, SuperCrude does not achieve the same nucleosynthetic yields as helmeos, motivating future work to improve the temperature accuracy further.
comments: ApJ Submitted

figs.cap: Comparison of pressure and energy density over a wide range of parameter space. Each curve represents a curve of constant density, varying temperature. Densities range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{10}$ g/cm$^{3}$, logarithmically in density, so that each curve is a factor of 100 higher density than the curve below it. Over this broad range of paramters, SuperCrude agrees broadly with the values computed by helmeos, in the sense that it captures the correct scaling and order-of-magnitude in each regime. Detailed errors are measured in later figures.

Relative error in pressure as a function of temperature $P(T)$ (top panel) and pressure as a function of energy density $P(\mathcal{E})$ (bottom panel). The function $P(\mathcal{E})$ is the closure equation needed by Euler’s equations. Its smaller errors are due to the fact that the ratio $P/\mathcal{E}$ is much more precisely maintained by SuperCrude than the exact functional form of $P(T)$.

Comparison in the measured entropy between SuperCrude and helmeos. SuperCrude’s entropy is internally self-consistent, in that an adiabatic process should preserve its definition of entropy exactly. Densities range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{10}$ g/cm$^{3}$, logarithmically in density, so that neighboring curves are separated by a factor of 100 in density.

Deviation of the SuperCrude model from the exact solution is evident in measurement of the heat capacity. Purple and blue dashed curves represent specific heats of $1.5(1+Z)k/m_{u}$ (electron + ion gas) and $1.5k/(Am_{u})$ (ion gas), respectively. The transition in the electrons from the gas phase to the degeneracy phase is the source of the largest errors in SuperCrude. Note that for the radiation-dominated phase, the pair plasma transition at $10^{9}$ K is visible in this plot. Densities range from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{10}$ g/cm$^{3}$, logarithmically in density, so that neighboring curves are separated by a factor of 100 in density.

Measurement of the hydrodynamically relevant ratio of pressure to energy, defined as $\Gamma_{H}=1+P/\mathcal{E}$. Regions of parameter space with a constant value of $\Gamma_{H}$ are reasonably well-approximated by an adiabatic equation of state. Both SuperCrude and helmeos transition from a $5/3$ law at low temperatures and densities to a $4/3$ law at high temperatures and densities. Note also the dip below $4/3$ at $10^{9}$ K, which is caused by the creation of electron-positron pairs, which (at these temperatures) contribute their rest mass to the energy density, but not as significantly to the pressure.

Comparison of the effective adiababatic index $\Gamma_{1}=(\partial{\rm ln}P/\partial{\rm ln}\rho)_{s}$. $\Gamma_{1}$ is another measure of the equation of state particularly relevant to hydrodynamical evolution and stability. In both codes it is measured via $\Gamma_{1}=c_{s}^{2}\rho h/P$; as such $\Gamma_{1}$ also measures the accuracy in computation of the sound speed. SuperCrude performs similarly in computing $\Gamma_{1}$ as it does with $\Gamma_{H}$ (Figure 5). One minor additional point to note: at very high temperatures and low densities, $\Gamma_{1}$ asymptotes to $4/3$ as the sound speed asymptotes to $c/\sqrt{3}$. However, helmeos appears to exhibit minor numerical noise in this regime, giving 0.1% level errors at very high temperatures (see lower panel). In this regime, we are unable measure the true $\Gamma_{1}$ error in SuperCrude, but it is below the 0.1% level.

title: Reconciling Giant Impacts with the Radius Valley: The Role of Silicate-Hydrogen Miscibility for Sub-Neptunes
authors: Eva Zlimen, Hilke E. Schlichting, James G. Rogers
abstract: Giant impacts are believed to play a major role in the assembly, long-term orbital stability, and resonant structure of exoplanetary systems. We revisit giant impact driven atmospheric escape while chemically coupling the interior and atmosphere by allowing for silicate-hydrogen miscibility. Incorporating hydrogen-silicate miscibility fundamentally alters atmospheric escape compared to chemically-inert models. While previous work on chemically-inert planets has found sub-Neptunes to undergo total atmospheric loss following collisions with impactors only a tenth of their mass, we find that including silicate-hydrogen miscibility can significantly reduce mass loss. This results from an increased envelope mean molecular weight, interior hydrogen sequestration, and modified compositional gradients in miscible planets. Miscible planets sequester hydrogen in their interiors post-impact, reducing the hydrogen available in the envelope for mass loss. As planets cool, hydrogen exsolves into their envelopes. Because more massive planets cool slower, they sequester hydrogen for longer, undergoing less mass loss. Thus, atmospheric retention depends more strongly on planet mass than impact energy, provided the impact does not gravitationally unbind the planet. Planets with masses $\gtrsim$4.50 $M_{\oplus}$ and hydrogen mass fractions > 5 % typically retain atmospheres of several percent after a giant impact, while planets with masses $\lesssim$3.30 $M_{\oplus}$ are almost entirely stripped of their envelopes. This allows sub-Neptunes with hydrogen-dominated envelopes to survive giant impacts. Contrastingly, lower-mass planets, which ultimately populate the super-Earth regime, are frequently stripped of their envelopes. Our findings suggest that super-Earths and sub-Neptunes could originate from a single population with rocky interiors even if post-disk-dispersal giant impacts were common.
comments: 12 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to MNRAS

figs.cap: Interior structure of a 4.09 $M_{\oplus}$ miscible (pink) and chemically-inert (orange) target planet before (dashed) and after (solid) an impact to yield a 4.50 $M_{\oplus}$ planet. Mass, pressure, temperature, density $\rho$, mean molar weight $\mu$, and hydrogen mass fraction $f_{H_{2}}$ are shown vs radius, in $R_{\oplus}$, out to the photospheric radius. The post-impact RCB is indicated by filled circles. Following an impact, the chemically-inert planet is inflated to a larger radius without greatly altering the size of the interior, while the miscible planet has a more extended interior. The density (lower left panel) of the miscible planet interior is greatly reduced post-impact due to an increase of hydrogen within it. As seen in the bottom right panel, the miscible planet has a more gradual compositional gradient in hydrogen content than the chemically-inert one as it transitions from a silicate-dominated interior to hydrogen-dominated envelope.

Post-impact time evolution of a 4.50 $M_{\oplus}$ planet with an equilibrium temperature of 500 K formed from a collision between a 4.09 $M_{\oplus}$ target planet and 0.41 $M_{\oplus}$ impactor for both a miscible (pink) and chemically-inert (orange) case. Shown in the first column is the time evolution of the photospheric radius R$_{p}$ while in the second column is the mass loss rate as a fraction of the initial hydrogen mass. In the third column is the time evolution of the interior hydrogen mass fraction (dashed) and total planet hydrogen mass fraction (solid). The fraction of hydrogen remaining is indicated on the right axis. Immediately post-impact, the miscible planet sequesters the majority of its hydrogen in the interior, thus preventing extreme core-powered mass loss. In contrast, the standard, chemically-inert model has twice the radius of the miscible model and several orders of magnitude higher mass loss rates post-impact. Note that the mass loss rate of the miscible model sharply decreases at $\sim 10^{6}$ years. Here, mass loss is limited by the rate at which hydrogen can exsolve from the interior. This is due to depletion of hydrogen within the envelope. Once sufficient hydrogen has exsolved from the interior, mass loss can proceed more rapidly.

Schematic of hydrogen exsolving from the interior of a miscible planet following a giant impact. In column a), immediately post-impact, the planet has an inflated silicate-dominated interior (orange) storing the majority of its hydrogen. A small hydrogen-dominated envelope (pink) sits atop the interior. While this envelope has a high density at the outer radius of the planet (black dashes), defined by the minimum of Bondi and Hill radii, the mass of the envelope itself is small. As core-powered mass loss proceeds through column b), the small available envelope is lost as the interior cools. Both processes drive the radius of the planet to shrink. This new, less energetic state is shown in column c), where hydrogen can now exsolve from the interior to replenish the envelope. At this point, the planet is less inflated than it was immediately post-impact, allowing for lower densities at the outer radius and consequently a lower mass loss rate.

Total hydrogen fraction lost over time vs post-impact planet mass for chemically-inert (orange) and miscible (pink) models following impacts with impactors of 0.1$M_{t}$, where $M_{t}$ is the mass of the target planet. Loss due to the impact shock is shown as the black dotted line (Eq. 33 of Schlichting et al. 2015), which is only important for higher mass miscible planets. Planets are assumed to initially have 5% hydrogen envelopes. As planet mass increases, the amount of hydrogen lost is reduced substantially in the miscible case. Higher mass miscible planets undergo negligible mass loss.

Fraction of hydrogen stored in the interior immediately post-impact vs post-impact planet mass for chemically-inert (orange) and miscible (pink) models following impacts with impactors of 0.1$M_{t}$, where $M_{t}$ is the mass of the target planet. Planets are assumed to initially have 5% hydrogen envelopes. For miscible planets, planet mass controls how much hydrogen can be stored in the interior immediately post-impact. More massive miscible planets can sequester more hydrogen within the interior, and so undergo less mass loss.

Fraction of hydrogen stored in the interior immediately post-impact (left) and total hydrogen fraction lost over time (right) versus impact velocity as a fractional increase of the mutual escape velocity for miscible (pink) and chemically-inert (orange) planets of different masses. Planets are assumed to initially have 5% hydrogen envelopes. For miscible planets, mass loss is reduced as planet mass increases. While increasing the impact velocity increases the amount of hydrogen stored in the interior immediately post-impact, little difference is seen in mass loss between different impact velocities. Further increases in impact velocity do not affect the hydrogen fraction lost.

title: A morpho-kinematic view of the Necklace nebula
authors: E. Santamaría, J.A. Toalá, L. Sabin, M. A. Guerrero, G. Ramos-Larios
abstract: We present a morpho-kinematic study of the Necklace Nebula based on spatially resolved spectroscopic observations and 3D modeling performed with the SHAPE software. The nebula is characterized by an equatorial disrupted ring accompanied by bipolar outflows. The geometry and velocity field of these different components are derived from the comparison between observed and synthetic images and position-velocity diagrams. The best model successfully reproduces the main morphological and kinematic features of the nebula, allowing us to constrain its 3D structure. We confirm that the disrupted ring is tilted about 60° from the plane of the sky, but the bipolar outflows are inclined by 46° with respect to the line of sight. This situation might indicate that the bipolar structures are not simple extensions of the equatorial ring, but instead correspond to a distinct mass-ejection event. The slight misalignment between these two components suggests either precession of the ejection axis, a temporal change in the dominant mass-loss geometry, or a misalignment in the magnetic field. Given that the Necklace Nebula hosts a close binary central star and is a well-established post-common envelope planetary nebula, our results support a scenario in which binary interaction plays a central role in shaping its morphology, even before the common envelope phase.
comments: 10 pages, 6 figures and 2 tables. Accepted in MNRAS

title: Mg II Signatures of Frequency Dependent Wave Propagation in Magnetic Elements
authors: Deborah Baker, David M. Long, Marco Stangalini, Michele Berretti, Andy S. H. To, Stephanie L. Yardley, Paola Testa
abstract: Waves in solar magnetic elements provide a pathway for transporting and dissipating energy in the chromosphere, yet the relationship between photospheric oscillations and chromospheric spectral structure remains incompletely understood. We investigate whether distinct chromospheric Mg II spectral states are linked to different populations of photospheric kink mode oscillations, with particular focus on the role of high frequency (~5mHz) waves. Magnetic elements are tracked in SDO/HMI magnetograms to derive horizontal velocity power spectra, while corresponding Mg II h + k profiles from IRIS are classified using k-means clustering into morphology-based (SHAPE) and intensity-based (ABS) groups. Both classifications exhibit systematic differences in oscillatory behavior. The SHAPE clusters isolate spectral morphologies associated with enhanced high-frequency power, including cases where oscillations in the 4-6 mHz band exceed those in the photospheric p-mode band. In contrast, the ABS clusters show a monotonic increase in the relative contribution of high-frequency oscillations with increasing emission strength and magnetic flux. These results indicate that high-frequency oscillations are both selectively enhanced in specific chromospheric states and systematically strengthened in stronger magnetic environments. This suggests that magnetic structuring plays a key role in regulating both the transmission and the conversion of kink mode wave energy into observable chromospheric signatures.
comments: Submitted to Solar Physics. 22 pages, 4 figures

title: Odds Estimation for Supermassive Black Hole Binaries in Local Core Galaxies
authors: C.J. Harris, Kayhan Gültekin
abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) are expected products of massive galaxy mergers, but identifying binaries in nearby galaxies remains challenging. We combine simulated massive-galaxy assembly histories from IllustrisTNG with a semi-analytic core-scouring model to connect observable core galaxy properties to the probability of hosting a bound SMBHB at z=0. We (i) construct a core galaxy population using an observationally motivated galaxy stellar mass function, (ii) model binary evolution through dynamical friction, stellar hardening, and gravitational-wave emission, and (iii) perform logistic regressions with five observable predictors: stellar mass deficit, stellar mass, central density, central velocity dispersion, and effective radius. The resulting models perform well on simulated systems, achieving a pseudo-$R^2$ of $0.51\pm0.03$, accuracy $0.95\pm0.01$, precision $0.92\pm0.03$, and recall $0.82\pm0.04$. Uncoalesced binaries are typically compact, with separations peaking near 0.3 pc, though only $\sim0.3\%$ emit in the pulsar timing array band. Applying the model to observed core galaxies, we identify eight nearby galaxies more likely than not to host SMBHBs. Of those eight host candidates, we note Messier 86 (NGC 4406) as a particularly likely example that was similarly identified using independent means and therefore warrants future follow-up.
comments: 18 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, submitted to AAS Journals

figs.cap: The purple solid curve shows the local galaxy stellar mass function used to down-sample the catalog of IllustrisTNG subhalos used in our core-formation model. It is described by a single Schechter function whose normalization, amplitude, and index controlling the sharpness of the transition from low- to high-mass are selected to be consistent with the nanohertz gravitational-wave background. The pink shaded region depicts the 16% and 84% confidence regions. The black data points with error bars show the mean core galaxy stellar mass function (above $10^{10}M_{\odot}$) produced by our model across 1000 iterations.

We show the feature space distributions according to single (blue) or binary (orange) occupation. The histograms show the binned posteriors, while the smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The shaded region shows the 16% and 84% confidence region. Colored points represent the eight model-selected candidates described in section V.1. The feature distributions are well separated, indicating that they are informative for the logistic classifier. The lack of significant covariance between features reflects low variance-inflation factors and allows the derived regression coefficients to be interpreted physically.

We show the logistic regression coefficient posteriors for 1000 iterations of our core-scouring model. The distributions are well constrained, capturing robust information about host properties that result in surviving binaries. The histograms show the binned posteriors, while the smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The shaded region shows the 16% and 84% confidence region, while the dashed lines show the maximum-likelihood estimate for each coefficient. The 2D histograms show the covariances for each coefficient, which appear as expected for low variance-inflation factors among the features. We find the maximum likelihood values of the coefficients to be ${\cal A}=-2.17,\ {\cal B}=-2.54,\ {\cal C}=1.80,$ and ${\cal D}=-3.77$.

The predicted separation distribution for dual (pink) and binary (orange) SMBHs in local core galaxies. The histograms show the binned $z=0$ separations of each black hole pair across 1000 iterations of our core-scouring model. The smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The shaded regions show the 16% and 84% intervals and the dashed lines show the maximum-likelihood estimates. Duals in the model tend to cluster around the initial separation, pointing to low stellar densities and inefficient dynamical friction in the host galaxies. Binary separations peak at subparsec distances. At larger separations ($\sim 10^{1}$–$10^{3}$ pc) hardening is efficient and pairs spend little time in this regime.

The distributions of total black hole mass, mass ratio, and present-day separation for binaries across all model realizations (orange) alongside distributions of black hole mass and mass ratio for single SMBHs at $z=0$ (blue). Histograms show the binned data while smooth curves are kernel density estimations. The dashed lines show the maximum-likelihood estimates while shaded regions show the 16 and 84 percentiles. Surviving binaries tend to have higher total mass and lower mass ratio than those which have coalesced, reflecting assembly via hierarchical merging. Present-day binaries with higher total mass tend to exist at larger separations.

The histogram shows the posterior distribution of circular gravitational wave frequencies of surviving binaries across all model outputs. The smooth curve is a kernel density estimate with the purple shaded region indicating the 16 to 84 percentile range. The dashed line shows the most likely frequency ($2.1\times 10^{-10}\ {\rm Hz}$). The pink shaded region shows the frequency space pulsar timing arrays are sensitive to. Only a small portion of all $z=0$ binaries in the model (0.3%) are active as pulsar timing array sources. Most binaries are either too widely separated or else have already evolved past the relevant regime.

title: Detailed chemo-dynamical characterization of four elusive Milky Way star clusters
authors: D. A. Alvarez Garay, E. Ceccarelli, D. Massari, M. Bellazzini, A. Mucciarelli, M. Libralato, E. Pancino, A. Avdeeva, M. Echeveste, E. I. Leitinger, S. Nedhath, S. Rani, E. Reggiani, N. Sanna, S. Saracino, L. Steinbauer, A. Turchi, E. Dodd, E. R. Garro, C. Zerbinati
abstract: A variety of faint and observationally challenging stellar systems has been discovered in the Milky Way in the last decades. Unveiling their kinematic and chemical properties is crucial to understand their nature and to assess their role in the history of our Galaxy. In this paper, we present a chemo-dynamical analysis of four elusive stellar systems (BH 140, Garro 01, BLISS 1, and Kim 3) using spectra collected with the X-shooter medium-resolution spectrograph at the VLT. We derived precise line-of-sight velocities and chemical abundances for all targets. Specifically, we provide the first spectroscopic characterization of metallicity and {\alpha}-element content for BH 140, the first comprehensive chemical characterization for BLISS 1 and Garro 01, and the first spectroscopic metallicity determination for Kim 3. BH 140, Garro 01 and BLISS 1 are relatively metal-rich systems with [Fe/H] ~ -0.7 dex and have enhanced {\alpha}-element abundances, whereas Kim 3 is notably metal-poor with [Fe/H] ~ -1.8 dex. We also performed an orbital analysis to investigate their origin as accreted or in situ systems. We found that Garro 01 and BH 140 have orbits confined within < 1.5 kpc from the Galactic plane, the former having also a remarkably circular orbit. They were likely born in situ, although the high orbital eccentricity of BH 140 and its mild deficiency in {\alpha}-elements leave other possibilities open. Although undoubtedly accreted, BLISS 1 does not exhibit a clear dynamical association with any known progenitor, lying in a high energy (E) - high vertical angular momentum (LZ ) prograde orbit reaching a maximum height from the Galactic plane of zmax ~ 8 kpc. Its chemical properties seem to favor an in situ origin, which might be connected with the Aleph sub-structure. Finally, we tentatively link the high energy and low LZ orbit of Kim 3 to the Elqui stream.
comments: Accepted for publication in A&A

The black triangles represent the in situ GCs, the green squares the GCs associated with GSE, the purple circles the GCs associated with Sgr dSph, and the light-gray circles the GCs associated with other progenitors.

Portions of the X-shooter spectra for four stars of BH 140 (red solid line), BLISS 1 (blue solid line), Garro 01 (green solid line), and Kim 3 (orange solid line) around some lines of interest (Mg and Fe). The lines of interest for the chemical analysis are marked as dashed vertical lines.

title: 3-Methoxy-1-propanol Rotational Spectroscopy and Radio Astronomical Search toward NGC 6334I
authors: D. Archie Stewart, Laurent Margulès, Roman A. Motiyenko, Brett A. McGuire
abstract: The methoxy functionalized alcohol species methoxymethanol and 2-methoxyethanol have recently been identified toward the MM1 protostellar source in the NGC 6334I massive star-forming region. Here we report measurements of portions of the centimeter, millimeter, and sub-millimeter regions of the rotational spectrum of the most stable conformer of 3-methoxy-1-propanol in order to probe the presence of even larger methoxylated alcohols toward the source. The experimental rotational parameters determined from these spectra were used to simulate the rotational spectrum of 3-methoxy-1-propanol under the physical conditions of the MM1 source and compared to the same ALMA observational dataset of the source in which 2-methoxyethanol was first discovered. No 3-methoxy-1-propanol transitions are identified in the data, and an upper limit on its column density toward the source was determined to be $7.5 \cdot 10^{15} \text{ cm}^{-2}$. When considering the series of these three methoxy alcohols, the decrease in column density going from 2-methoxyethanol to 3-methoxy-1-propanol is consistent with how the column density of 2-methoxyethanol decreases compared to methoxymethanol.

figs.cap: The estimated transition frequency errors in the 3-methoxypropanol catalog extrapolated from the cm-wave measurements. The upper portion of the plot overlaps with the 130–145 GHz range of the ALMA observations of NGC 6334I where it can be seen that the frequencies of the strongest transitions within the observational range are expected to be poorly predicted.

A Loomis-Wood plot of the $K_{a}=0$ a-type transitions of 3-methoxypropanol in the 150–170 GHz range. Each row shows a 30 MHz wide region of the experimental spectrum centered at the transition frequencies predicted by the cm-wave rotational parameters. The relevant quantum numbers are listed by the left edge of the plot above the simulated transition frequency (MHz) and simulated intensity (unitless). In this format, the actual frequencies of the selected transitions are easily identified in the six peaks in the right half of the plot that align in a nearly linear pattern. This linear patterns arises from the simulated transition frequencies steadily becoming more inaccurate due to errors in the rotational parameters as the $J$ levels of the transition increase.

In red, the rotational spectrum of 3-methoxypropanol is simulated at a column density of $8\cdot 10^{16}\text{ cm}^{-2}$ against the black observational data of the MM1 peak in NGC 6334I. Although there is some overlap between the simulation and observational data, the rotational spectrum of 3-methoxypropanol is not present in the observational data. The large peaks in the simulation are blends of multiple rotational transitions, and the corresponding energy levels of these transitions are labeled with Greek letters where: $\alpha=\{0,1\}$, $\beta=\{1,2\}$, and $\gamma=\{13,14\}$

The relative energies of the five isomers of methoxypropanol, computed by the AIMNet2 neural network model [21]. Each isomer is depicted in its most stable geometry. In most isomers, there is some stabilizing interaction between the -OH group and a lone pair of electrons in the -OCH$_{3}$ group. In 3-methoxypropanol, the groups are far enough apart that a pseudo six membered ring can form via an intramolecular hydrogen bond. This noncovalent hydrogen bond is indicated with a dashed line.

title: Running cosmological constant in light of recent CMB-BAO data
authors: A. Racioppi, M. Vijar
abstract: We revisit single-field slow-roll inflation driven by a running cosmological constant, i.e. a cosmological constant receiving a logarithmic radiative correction, in light of the latest CMB-BAO data. The relative radiative correction $\delta$ is treated as a free parameter of the model and allowed to be positive or negative. For positive $\delta$, the predictions interpolate between a logarithmic regime and a linear inflation one. Compatibility with CMB-only data is confined to a narrow stripe near the $2\sigma$ border where $\delta$ is relatively large. On the other hand, the predictions fit easily within the constraints including BAO data in a wide range of parameters. For negative $\delta$, the slow-roll approximation breaks down at small field values and the predictions are excluded by data. However, once the effective mass contribution inside the logarithmic correction is taken into account, the negative $\delta$ potential develops a local maximum and behaves like a hilltop model, achieving compatibility with CMB-only data, while agreement with CMB-BAO data is possible only at $2\sigma$.
comments: 15 pages, 5 figures

title: Flow-based neural networks for scalable high resolution imaging of VLBI observations
authors: Lev Kats, Alexey Goldin, Andrey S. Andrianov
abstract: Bayesian sampling methods in very-long-baseline interferometry enable reliable imaging of astronomical sources with a record high angular resolution. However, even after the transition from classical MCMC methods to flow-based neural networks, they remain computationally expensive as the number of recovered features grows. We used WaveletFlow neural network architecture to increase the number of pixels in the recovered image distribution, addressing the scaling issues of previous models. We applied the algorithm to both model data and archive RadioAstron project observations of M87 and ALMA telescope observations of HL Tau. While yielding comparable fidelity of the individual images, the algorithm provides more statistical information compared to CLEAN, which may be crucial for future research on compact astronomical objects such as active galactic nuclei.
comments: Published in MNRAS

figs.cap: Affine coupling block. The input is first divided into two disjoint slices in the channel dimension or using checkerboard masks. Then, the first slice concatenated with the conditioning are passed to a general convolutional neural network to modify the second slice. Finally, the first slice and modified second slice are concatenated back to produce the output.

FlowNet architecture, which consists of repeated blocks of invertible convolutions, couplings (optionally conditioned) and actnorm layers. Each block starts with reshape layer: it transforms an $N\times C\times H\times W$ image into $N\times 16C\times H/4\times W/4$, and ends with another one that reshapes the image back to $N\times C\times H\times W$. Note that in the second coupling layer, the inputs are swapped.

WaveletFlow sampling process, which starts with generating a ’coarse’ image and first DWT coefficients and results in an image that is constrained to be positive. Arrows with circles denote conditioning.

title: Simultaneous Real-Color Time-Domain Survey of the Coma Field with the Multi-channel Photometric Survey Telescope (Mephisto)
authors: Yu Pan, Yuan-Pei Yang, Ye-Hao Cheng, Brajesh Kumar, Jie-Wei Zhao, Yongzhi Cai, Xinlei Chen, Jian Cui, Guowang Du, Yuan Fang, Helong Guo, Panpan Huang, Kaushik Chatterjee, Ziwei Li, Jianhui Lian, Chenxu Liu, Xiangkun Liu, Chenxi Shang, Tao Wang, Chunsheng Xiao, Jinghua Zhang, Kong-Jun Zhang, Shiyan Zhong, Zihao Zhou, Dan Zhu, Xufeng Zhu, Xingzhu Zou, Xiaowei Liu
abstract: We present the results from a high-cadence, multi-channel time-domain survey targeting the Coma galaxy cluster, utilizing the newly commissioned 1.6-m Multi-channel Photometric Survey Telescope (Mephisto). Mephisto's pioneering mosaic focal-plane design enables strictly simultaneous imaging in three distinct optical bands ($u/v, g/r, i/z$). This unique capability allows for the extraction of true, instantaneous spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of fast-evolving transients. Our survey continuously monitors a 20-square-degree footprint centered on the Coma cluster. By strategically targeting this massive local structure, we exploit cosmic anisotropy to significantly amplify the volumetric discovery rate of stellar explosions. During the initial six-month pilot operation, we successfully detected and tracked nine new supernovae (SNe). Remarkably, our high-cadence, multi-band strategy allowed us to capture ultra-early rising light curves and pre-discovery signals (e.g., SN 2026dyr) hours to days prior to formal discovery alerts. These instantaneous early-phase colors allow us to reconstruct intrinsic SEDs without temporal interpolation, providing reliable constraints on the physical parameters of early supernova (SN) evolution. Furthermore, our observed supernova yield shows good agreement with theoretical forecasts based on local stellar mass and star-formation rate overdensities. These pilot results validate the efficiency of the Mephisto Coma survey, demonstrating its objective capability to systematically explore the local transient population and provide rapid optical localizations for future multi-messenger events.
comments: 14 pages, 9 figures and 3 tables. Comments welcome!

The number of observations in each photometric band for each field is indicated on the map. The blue stars mark the positions of the nine supernovae identified in the Coma field.

The data are available at Science Data Bank: https://doi.org/10.57760/sciencedb.014le

title: The Korean Space Telescope (KST): A Dedicated Space Observatory for the Dark Universe
authors: M. James Jee, Ho Seong Hwang, Dongwook Lim, Minjin Kim, Myungshin Im, Sungwook E. Hong, Ho-Gyu Lee, Soung-Chul Yang, David Parkinson, Arman Shafieloo, Jun-Qian Jiang, Haeng Pal Heo, Dongok Ryu, Hagyong Kihm, Hyung Yun Noh, Wooyong Kang, Youngsun Kim
abstract: The Korean Space Telescope (KST) is a next-generation 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory, a dedicated probe of the dark sector. Its single instrument provides diffraction-limited visible imaging (~0.15 arcsec in the optical) together with simultaneous near-infrared (R ~ 100) slitless spectrophotometry, so that every detected source is observed in the NIR by the survey itself, with spectral information delivered at a resolution set by its brightness (full R ~ 100 typing at the bright end, synthetic medium-band or broadband photometry below it) and with no separate follow-up, a capability decisive for time-domain science. With it, KST addresses the three outstanding questions of dark physics in concert: the dynamics of dark energy, the nature of dark matter, and gravitational-wave dark sirens as independent cosmological rulers. KST combines measurements of expansion and structure growth to test dark-energy models. A two-tiered "Wedding Cake" strategy (2,000 deg^2 Wide plus 10 deg^2 cluster-targeted Deep Survey) combines weak lensing, baryon acoustic oscillations, and a near-infrared-standardized Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy at its pivot redshift (sigma(w_p) ~ 0.03); maps dark matter from cluster cores to galactic substructure to test cold dark matter against warm and self-interacting alternatives; and builds a deep near-infrared host catalog for a distance-ladder-independent H_0 from dark sirens. The same data yield a Legacy Science portfolio (galaxy evolution, active galactic nuclei, exoplanets, and the Milky Way) at no additional observing cost. As Korea's first dedicated astrophysics space mission, KST occupies a niche complementary to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and Roman.
comments: 55 pages, 21 figures, 11 tables. White paper for the Korean Space Telescope (KST). To be Submitted to the Journal of the Korean Astronomical Society (JKAS)

figs.cap: Conceptual rendering of the Korean Space Telescope (KST) in its operational orbit. The spacecraft design leverages the high-resolution imaging and orbital stability heritage of the Korean Multi-Purpose Satellite (KOMPSAT) series (Lee et al., 2021b; Seo et al., 2020) to support a 1.4-meter wide-field astronomical surveyor.

Aperture optimization for the imaging channel. The survey grasp (etendue $\propto D^{-1}$; grey dashed) decreases with aperture, while the density of cleanly resolved and deblended galaxies in the visible (VIS) imaging channel (blue) increases as the PSF shrinks below the faint-galaxy size and then saturates. Their product, the rate at which science-usable galaxies are surveyed (red), has a genuine interior optimum at $D\approx 1.4$ m: the aperture whose $\sim 0.15^{\prime\prime}$ visible PSF matches the $\theta_{g}\sim 0.15^{\prime\prime}$ scale that must be resolved for faint-galaxy shape measurement and deblending. Below this the PSF blends the faint population and degrades shapes; above it, survey grasp is spent resolving already-resolved sources. Curves are peak-normalized; the construction is an illustrative design rationale, with the model and its inputs given in Section 2. The near-infrared channel provides $R\sim 100$ spectrophotometry (photometric redshifts and SEDs), not imaging, and is not what sets the imaging optimum.

Schematic of the KST dichroic beam splitter and detector mosaics. The common incident beam is separated into simultaneous VIS and NIR channels. (a) Four CMOS detectors form a $4\times 1$ mosaic, with one fixed $g$, $r$, $i$, or $z$ filter per detector. (b) Twenty-seven square H2RG detectors form a $9\times 3$ mosaic beneath an LVF whose transmission wavelength varies continuously from 1.1 to 1.8 $\mu$m along the scan direction, providing $R\approx 100$ spectral mapping. Green outlines mark the identical $1^{\circ}\times 0.25^{\circ}$ science fields; hatched regions indicate detector area outside the adopted field. Both mosaics are drawn on a common scale using the 19 m effective focal length and the specified pixel pitches. Detector gaps and H2RG reference-pixel borders are omitted. Beam routing and channel orientation are schematic, and relay optics are not shown.

KST sensitivity. (a) $5\sigma$ limiting AB magnitude versus wavelength for a 1-hr exposure. Filled circles show KST point-source depths in $g,r,i,z$ from a first-principles exposure-time calculator (ETC) calibrated to reproduce the tabulated depths (Table 1); open circles show the corresponding $0.3^{\prime\prime}$-galaxy depths. The orange bar marks the NIR LVF per-resolution-element ($R\sim 100$) continuum depth across $1.1$–$1.8~\mu$m, which is naturally shallower than broadband imaging. Grey squares show the Euclid Wide survey for comparison (filled: point source; open: extended VIS). (b) Point-source $5\sigma$ depth versus integration time for the four VIS bands; the dotted line and filled points mark the 1-hr survey depth. The ETC assumes a 1.4-m aperture with central obscuration, CDS read noise $<5\,e^{-}$, dark current, and a conservative zodiacal$+$Earthshine sky model (bounding the low-Earth-orbit case); the effective per-band throughput is calibrated to the point-source depths of Table 1.

The error budget, not the statistics, sets the constraint. Forecast $68\%$ confidence contours in the $w_{0}$–$w_{a}$ plane for the same KST survey under three error budgets, from the systematics-marginalized Fisher analysis described in the text: statistical precision only (blue); the KST error budget, with its internally measured shear calibration, mean-redshift, and NIR supernova systematics (red); and an otherwise identical survey carrying a conventional broadband systematics chain (orange dashed). Contours are centred on the $\Lambda$CDM fiducial (star); the prior widths defining the two chains are stated in the text. Marginalizing over systematics costs the conventional chain a factor $\sim$3 in figure of merit relative to KST’s. The KST-error-budget contour corresponds to $\sigma(w_{0})=0.096$, $\sigma(w_{a})=0.36$, FoM $=79$ ($\sigma(w_{p})\approx 0.035$ at the pivot), computed for the current survey ($5{,}000$ SNe to $z\approx 1$, $n_{\rm eff}=57$, $(1+z)$-scaled redshift-bias priors); the bridge to the full-probe headline forecasts is given in the text.

Histogram of confirmed exoplanets by discovery year and detection method. The annual number of confirmed exoplanets is shown, color-coded by detection method. Transit surveys dominate the overall discovery yield, with radial-velocity surveys providing the second-largest contribution, while microlensing, imaging, astrometry, and other methods probe complementary regions of parameter space. The rapid increase in confirmed planets in the mid-2010s illustrates the transformative role of space-based missions such as Kepler and K2. Adapted from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

title: A Low-Dimensional Chemical Representation of High-Resolution Stellar Disk Spectra: Residual Abundance Signatures
authors: Sarah E. Aquilina, Melissa K. Ness, Sven Buder
abstract: Stellar abundances are generated by complex chemical enrichment pathways yet show strong correlation structure. We test how well high-quality spectra of low-alpha disk stars can be reconstructed using low-dimensional models. By validating model performance in flux space, we quantify and locate where residual information persists. Using HARPS spectra (R = 115,000, SNR > 100) and labels derived with Korg, we train generative models (The Cannon) conditioned on stellar parameters Teff, log(g), [M/H], vsini, and vmic, and three abundance labels, [Ti/H], [Y/H], and [Nd/H], representing distinct nucleosynthetic families. Evaluating model performance on unseen test stars through flux residuals, the model reproduces the global spectra to a median residual amplitude of 0.3%. Deviations in 15 absorption features for unlabelled elements are typically < 0.7%. Residuals of ~1% correspond to abundance differences of 0.01-0.05 dex. Degrading the spectra to medium resolution (R = 28,000) decreases the median residual amplitude from 0.3% to 0.2%, redistributing the residual signal over the instrumental line profile. Our publicly available model reproduces features from 29 elements to sub-percent precision across -1.13 < [M/H] < 0.29. This demonstrates that the dominant chemical variation encoded in low-alpha disk spectra can be captured by a low-dimensional model, while weaker chemical information remains encoded in flux residuals. High-resolution, high-SNR spectra (R ~ 100,000, SNR > 100) are essential to resolve the hierarchical layers of chemical information beyond this low-dimensional structure. The model provides a benchmark for assessing the chemical information accessible to current surveys like 4MOST and GALAH 2, as well as upcoming facilities like VLT/HRMOS and GMT/G-CLEF.
comments: 32 pages, 41 figures

Black regions correspond to tellurics and the HARPS CCD gap ($5300-5340$ Å) removed prior to training. Note that all wavelengths are in the vacuum rest frame.

title: Harmonic brightness oscillations point to magnetar giant flares in rare short gamma-ray bursts
authors: Run-Chao Chen, Ore Gottlieb, Bin-Bin Zhang, Yuri Levin, Dong Lai, Jun Yang, Yi-Han Iris Yin, Suo-Ning Wang
abstract: Kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) have been observed in a few rare gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), but their physical origin remains uncertain. We reanalyze the two short GRBs with reported kilohertz QPOs, GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A, and find evidence for possible harmonic-like organization around a characteristic frequency scale near 360 hertz. The similar harmonic-like pattern in GRB 910711 and in the confirmed magnetar giant flare (MGF) event GRB 200415A, including features extending above 4 kilohertz, points to timing phenomenology on frequency scales relevant to magnetar oscillation modes. The temporal and spectral similarities between the two events and the difficulty of explaining these features in merger-driven scenarios favor an MGF-like interpretation of GRB 910711. This timing phenomenology may therefore provide an additional observational handle, complementary to spectral, temporal, and localization information, for distinguishing rare MGF-like transients from merger-driven GRBs.
comments: 57 pages, 9 figures; Authors' version of the article published in Science Advances, available at this https URL

figs.cap: Temporal similarities between GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A. Time axes are aligned to the peak of each burst, as identified in 0.1-ms resolution data. (A) Multi-instrument light curves in the 60–325 keV band, shown at 2-ms resolution. (B) Bayesian block segmentation of the light curves in panel A, highlighting the temporal structures of each burst. The prior probability[28] for the Bayesian block algorithm was set to $p_{0}=0.001$ to avoid over-segmentation of the global light curve morphology. Both bursts show a sharp, millisecond-scale initial spike followed by a weaker, sub-second tail. (C) Initial spikes of GRB 910711 (BATSE-LADs, 20 keV–1.9 MeV) and GRB 200415A (ASIM-LED, 20–400 keV) at 25 $\mu$s resolution. Bayesian blocks under the prior $p_{0}=0.1$ are overlaid as shaded regions: blue for GRB 910711, red for GRB 200415A. Both bursts show similar sub-millisecond variability with multiple pulses. The finest structure in GRB 200415A is revealed only when the prior is relaxed to 0.2, marked by the red arrow.

Low-frequency excesses associated with the reported kilohertz brightness oscillations in GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A. Left: Leahy-normalized power spectra[29] and Lomb–Scargle periodograms computed from 2-$\mu$s binned light curves in the interval [96, 106] ms (see Fig. 1C), shown for GRB 200415A (top) and GRB 910711 (bottom). The displayed frequency range is 100–5000 Hz, and the Lomb–Scargle periodograms are evaluated on an oversampled frequency grid with 10-Hz spacing. Both bursts exhibit prominent low-frequency excesses near 350 and 360 Hz (red dashed lines). Red arrows indicate previously reported kilohertz brightness oscillations[5, 6]; GRB 910711 additionally shows an excess near 2100 Hz, close to the $\approx$2132 Hz oscillation reported in GRB 200415A. Right: Monte Carlo assessment of the low-frequency excesses. Histograms show the null distributions of the maximum Lomb–Scargle power recovered within the same $260$–$460$ Hz search interval from $10^{5}$ synthetic light curves generated under two assumptions: a FRED-envelope null model (purple), representing pulse-envelope variability alone, and a PL+2QPO null model (blue), incorporating the previously reported kilohertz oscillatory excesses in the power spectrum. The red dashed line marks the observed maximum Lomb–Scargle power. Under the FRED-envelope null, the low-frequency excesses are not readily reproduced, with probabilities of $p_{\rm FRED}\approx 0.001$ for GRB 200415A and $0.051$ for GRB 910711. Once the previously reported kilohertz excesses are incorporated, the corresponding probabilities increase to $p_{\rm PL+2QPO}\approx 0.334$ and $0.155$, respectively, suggesting that the low-frequency excesses become less unexpected in the presence of the reported high-frequency oscillatory structure.

Harmonic analysis of the shared 360-Hz oscillation feature in GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A. Top: Light curves binned at 0.1 ms without energy selection are shown in the top panels, with corresponding spectrograms from 2-$\mu$s-binned data below. Blue contours mark the top 95% of the test statistics. Harmonic candidates appear during the initial spikes at integer multiples $n\times f$ with $f=360$ Hz simultaneously, with $n=1,3,5,6,11$ for GRB 910711 and $n=1,2,4,6,12$ for GRB 200415A. Bottom: Bispectrum of the initial spike of GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A over the interval [96, 106] ms (red-shaded region in top panel), computed with 50-$\mu$s bins. The frequency grid is refined to 10 Hz resolution through zero padding[69], and a Hamming window[68] is applied to reduce red-noise leakage. Brighter regions in the bispectrum indicate larger bispectral magnitudes, corresponding to stronger nonlinear coupling. Symbols $H(x,y)$ (equivalent to $H(y,x)$) denote harmonic features at the frequency pair $(x\times f,\,y\times f)$, representing nonlinear coupling between two oscillations. Such coupling generates power at $x\times f$, $y\times f$, and their sum $(x+y)\times f$ in the Fourier spectrum. Frequency pairs closely associated with the harmonic peaks in spectrograms are marked with red stars, indicating the presence of a consistent harmonic system in both events.

Reconstruction of the GRB 910711 light curve using a template derived from GRB 200415A. Gray curves show the observed light curves in the shared 60–325 keV energy band for GRB 200415A (Swift-BAT, panel A) and GRB 910711 (BATSE-LADs, panel B). Insets highlight the initial spikes; blue lines show the corresponding simulated light curves. (A) The orange line indicates the best-fit model for GRB 200415A. (B) The orange line shows a scaled version of the model in panel A, assuming a 40% increase in detector sensitivity and placing GRB 200415A at an effective distance of $\approx$8.75 Mpc. Shaded regions indicate the time intervals of the initial spike and the decaying tail, as determined by Bayesian blocks, in both the observed (gray) and simulated (blue) light curves.

Spectrograms of GRB 910711 and GRB 200415A. Light curves used for spectrogram analysis are binned at 100 $\mu$s resolution, with a frequency resolution of 10 Hz. The exponential decay constant is set as $c_{w}=\frac{1}{(2000~\text{Hz}\times 0.03~\text{s})^{2}}$. (A) Low-energy light curves of GRB 910711 (BATSE-LADs, energy channels 1–3) and GRB 200415A (Swift-BAT and ASIM-LED). (B) WWZ spectrograms derived from the low-energy light curves, computed with 1-ms time resolution. Darker regions indicate higher statistical significance of periodic signals. Red boxes denote the previously reported kHz QPOs[5, 6]; red arrows mark the shared $\approx$2160 Hz QPO seen in both bursts. (C) WWA spectrograms for the same light curves, computed with 0.2-ms time resolution. Darker regions indicate stronger modulation power. Red contours enclose the top 25% and 50% of the total WWA energy, highlighting the most energetically significant QPO components. (D) High-energy light curves of GRB 910711 (BATSE-LADs, energy channel 4) and GRB 200415A (ASIM-HED). (E) Same as panel B, but for the high-energy light curves. (F) Same as panel C, but for the high-energy light curves.

Monte Carlo tests of the bispectral harmonic-node structure. (A) Example comparison between the observed light curve and one synthetic FRED-envelope realization, together with the corresponding bispectral map and the joint harmonic statistic $S(f_{0})$. Red contours mark the local regions around the candidate harmonic coupling nodes used to evaluate the bispectral statistics. The observed data show a preference near $f_{0}=360$ Hz, while the example synthetic realization does not reproduce the same harmonic-node pattern. (B) Monte Carlo distributions from $10^{5}$ FRED-envelope synthetic light curves. The left panel shows the distribution of the preferred characteristic frequency, defined as the $f_{0}$ that maximizes the joint harmonic statistic over 260–460 Hz. The middle panel shows the distribution of the maximum joint statistic over this interval, and the right panel shows the distribution of the joint statistic evaluated specifically at $f_{0}=360$ Hz. Purple dashed lines mark the observed values. (C) Marginal distributions of grouped harmonic-node statistics at $f_{0}=360$ Hz. These panels show how different parts of the candidate harmonic structure contribute to the observed joint statistic. (D–F) Same as (A–C), but for GRB 200415A. Despite differences in the specific harmonic nodes recovered in the two bursts, both observed events favor a characteristic frequency close to 360 Hz and show enhanced joint harmonic statistics relative to the FRED-envelope null simulations.

title: XRISM/Resolve Study of Large Scale Properties in Tycho's Supernova Remnant
authors: Tyler E. Hanover, Mark D. Leising
abstract: Resolve, the microcalorimeter array aboard the X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM), provides an unprecedented spectral view of Tycho's Supernova Remnant (SNR). We fit the X-ray spectra of the five public archival XRISM observations of the SNR with a multi-component non-equilibrium ionization plasma model assuming spherical expansion and a uniform abundance pattern. For pointings away from the center of the object, we divide each into three spectra based on angular distance from the remnant's geometric center and fit all three simultaneously with the center-pointing observation. We tie elemental abundances together across all model components. We find that pseudo-spherical expansion fits well the Tycho SNR in the regions where Resolve has observed, although iron appears slower on the approaching side than the receding side. We also find that a close-to-uniform abundance pattern across the SNR is consistent with these data.
comments: 14 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables, submitted to ApJ
