title: Update on the Orbital Motion of Encke's Periodic Comet: Nongravitational Deceleration Gradually Gaining
authors: Zdenek Sekanina
abstract: The end of an era in cometary astronomy --- as the transition from a nongravitational acceleration to a deceleration in the motion of Encke's comet was advertised in a paper of mine five years ago --- has now turned into a new era, as recent computations of the comet's nongravitational orbits performed independently by S. Nakano (CBAT) and by D. Farnocchia (JPL) appear to suggest. The new values of parameter A_2, compatible both with each other and with the earlier values in my previous paper, show that the magnitude of the deceleration has continued to grow. Critically assessed are the controversial computations at the Minor Planet Center, which contradict the above results and imply that Encke's comet was reverting to the acceleration. A plot of the number of observations used in the orbital solutions as a function of time shows an exponential rise following the introduction of CCD arrays, but not after use of photography became common five or six decades earlier. Dips in observer activity appear during the two World Wars. Because the comet has recently been observed along the entire orbit, the effective times that computed values of the nongravitational parameters apply to had to be redefined.
comments: 6 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables

figs.cap: Plot of the number of observations used per orbital solution for Encke’s comet, linking consecutive apparitions to determine the nongravitational parameters $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$. The numbers are normalized to an orbital arc of 13 years, equivalent approximately to four revolutions about the Sun, linking five consecutive apparitions. The plot shows an exponential rise in the number following the introduction of CCD arrays, as well as dips in observer activity during World War 1 and World War 2, when Encke’s 1944 return was missed. No increase of activity appears to have been associated with expanded use of photography from the 1920s on.

Variations in the nongravitational parameter $A_{2}$ of Encke’s comet over the past 50 years. Values in units of 10$^{-12}$ AU/day$^{2}$, derived as part of Style II nongravitational orbital solutions linking consecutive apparitions of the comet (Table 3), are plotted as solid circles, whose diameters are in proportion to the length of the orbital arc used. The shortest arc measures 7.8 years or 2.4 revolutions about the Sun, the longest 16.4 years or 5 revolutions. It is noted that the new additions, at 2020.5 (Nakano’s data point) and 2022.8 (Farnocchia’s data point), are compatible with the earlier values, showing that the nongravitational deceleration has recently continued to increase with time. The data in the plot are fitted by a quadratic polynomial (solid curve) and by a polynomial spline (dotted curve). The two curves are seen to extrapolate beyond 2023 very differently, suggesting that a future trend of the nongravitational perturbations of the motion of Encke’s comet cannot at present be accurately predicted, except that the deceleration is expected to continue to grow in magnitude.

title: A universal relation predicts the observed reversal of a supernova chirp
authors: Joseph R. Farah, Logan J. Prust, Hang Yu
abstract: Superluminous supernovae, among the brightest stellar explosions, are thought to be powered by newborn magnetars. One such event, SN 2024afav, ``chirped'', displaying sinusoidal, increasing-frequency ($P(99\textrm{ d})\sim39\pm8$ d to $P(166\textrm{ d})\sim17\pm5$ d) light-curve modulations. The model explaining this chirp, a precessing disk falling onto the dimming magnetar, generalizes to a normalization-independent universal relation between the period derivative and the dimming rate of the light curve. Applied to the published chirp alone, with the spin-down time measured from the unmodulated light curve, the relation predicts that the chirp must halt near $t \approx 150$ d and reverse. With continued follow-up of SN 2024afav, we report the discovery of five new modulations in which the chirp reverses ($P(177\textrm{ d})\sim24\pm4$ d to $P(208\textrm{ d})\sim38\pm2$ d) at $t=147\pm3$ d, as predicted. Applied to chirping events from upcoming surveys, the relation could identify the precession mechanism and disk physics of each engine.
comments: 17 pages, 8 figures

figs.cap: Magnetar model fit to SN 2024afav. We fit the magnetar model of [26] to the full ATLAS and LCO light curve of SN 2024afav using MOSFiT [22]. Uncertainties after MJD 60703 are inflated to absorb the impact of the modulations so they do not drive the fit. We find that the light curve out to $\sim 250$ days post-explosion is well-described as powered by the spin-down of a magnetar with spin period $P_{\rm spin}\sim 4$ ms and magnetic field strength $B\sim 0.5\times 10^{14}$ G. However, the smooth post-peak decline of the magnetar model does not explain the presence of 6–7 post-peak modulations in the light curve. The vertical dashed line at $\approx 175$ d post-explosion indicates the terminating epoch of the dataset of the previous analysis, which characterized the modulations at $t\lesssim 170$ d as a “chirp”.

Timing of the modulations. The post-peak light curve of SN 2024afav shows multiple significant modulations. Here, we characterize their timing using the bolometric luminosity as fit from the multi-band photometry following [31]. The chirp reported in the previous work (data left of the indicated purple line in panels A and B) is clearly recovered, with $\sim 3$ cycles of a chirping modulation visible. After approximately $t=170$ d, several new modulations are visible in the residual (data subtracted from a smoothing cubic spline) and the unsubtracted light curve. The late-time modulations display extrema spaced increasingly far apart, reproduced in a weighted wavelet z-transform [18] refined via the method of synchrosqueezing [11] (panel C, see subsection B.1). The evolution of the late-time modulations mirrors the originally-reported chirp, and its peaks and troughs are well-described by a sinusoid (blue curve, panel B; dashed blue line, panel C) whose period evolution is a symmetric parabola centered at $t\approx 158$ d. We phenomenologically characterize this new set of modulations as an “antichirp” due to the lengthening period.

The predicted chirp reversal is observed. We compare the predicted chirp reversal to the late-time modulations observed in SN 2024afav. The universal relation of Equation 1, when fit only to the chirp reported in previous work (panel A, blue points; end of previous analysis shown as dashed line), that a minimum should be present in the period at $t_{\rm min}\approx 133$ d (rest frame; value inferred from mode of $t_{\rm min}$ posterior distribution inferred from the chirp only shown in panel B, blue) and should culminate in an antichirp with approximate period derivative $\dot{P}=0.22^{+0.24}_{-0.11}$ (panel A, blue line and shaded region). After correcting for diffusion through the ejecta and converting the observed extrema timing into the rest frame of SN 2024afav, we find that the new modulations are consistent with this prediction at $\lesssim 1\sigma$ (panel B). The late-time modulations (orange points), when fit in conjunction with the chirp reported previously result in a minimum at $t_{\rm min}=132\pm 3$ d (panel B, orange distribution) and produce $\dot{P}=0.28\pm 0.12$ (orange line and spread). Finally, the period evolution displayed by the late-time modulations definitively rules out a continuation of the near-linear decline displayed by the periods which make up the chirp (dot-dashed line). Errorbars denote $1\sigma$ uncertainties on the period, constructed following subsection A.4.

Discreteness of the universal relation. The universal relation is constructed almost entirely from discretized quantities whose values represent specific configurations of the system. This quantization results in a finite set of lines against which the best-fit line traced by a supernova in the ($D$, $C$) space can be checked without requiring a fit, providing both a diagnostic as well as a falsifiability criterion. Indeed, we find that no line on the thin-disk (radiatively-cooling) comb (panel A) produces a slope as steep as SN 2024afav, statistically rejecting the thin-disk prescription for this object (best-fit closure—quadrupole-driven nodal precession (QDNP)—gives reduced $\chi^{2}=9.8$, $p=3\times 10^{-15}$). By contrast, a thick-disk (advective) prescription (panel B) can reproduce the observed slope and intercept in SN 2024afav (at $\lesssim 0.2\sigma$) with Lense-Thirring precession (LTP). Future chirping objects can be classified and characterized in this way. In Panel A, black lines indicate the best-match closure for each mechanism, while gray lines indicate the remaining closure menu (see Table 1). In Panel B, black lines indicate the $\chi=5/3$ [14] configurations, while gray lines indicate their $\chi=4/3$ [37] counterparts.
Magnetar model fit posterior. We show the results of the magnetar model fit described in subsection A.2 via a corner plot of the posterior conditioned on the full SN 2024afav light curve.

Are the SN 2024afav modulations likely to be red noise? A common explanation for modulations in SLSNe-I is interaction with randomly-distributed shells of CSM. We test this explanation against the modulations observed in SN 2024afav, which have two unique features relative to other SLSNe. First, they are unusually high-amplitude, and second, they produce a chirp followed by an antichirp. We constructed a synthetic red noise power spectrum by modeling the post-peak modulations of six SLSNe-I as red noise and generating $\sim 5\times 10^{4}$ realizations similar to SN 2024afav’s photometric uncertainty and cadence (examples shown in panel C). We then measured the rms amplitude and extracted extrema timings in an identical manner to our procedure for SN 2024afav. We find that that SN 2024afav is an extreme outlier even in a red noise distribution tuned to modulations in SLSNe-I. The two-dimensional distribution of realizations in parabola contrast and modulation power is shown in panel B; the distribution of a joint score of rarity (constructed based on the $p$-value of each realization relative to the overall marginal distribution in modulation power or parabola contrast, then combining those scores via a log product) is shown in panel A. Fewer than 100 realizations were more extreme than SN 2024afav; a sample of these few are shown in panel D.

title: Insights into the Kinematic Evolution of Filament-Induced Jets: Coupling of Interchange and Flare Reconnection
authors: Zehao Tang, Xiaoli Yan, Zhike Xue, Jincheng Wang, Zhe Xu, Yadan Duan
abstract: Jets are ubiquitous eruptive activities in the solar atmosphere, playing an important role in mass transport, atmospheric heating, and energy supply. However, the triggering mechanism remains elusive. To reveal the fine process of jet evolution, we study a jet associated with a B-class flare that involves in two distinct stages. Analyzing the complete evolution of a solar jet captured by the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we clearly identify its dual-stage kinematics, evolving from interchange to flare reconnection. This dual-stage jet is characterized by distinct dual-stage signatures in magnetic morphology, H$\alpha$ profile, jet speed, jet height, X-ray flux, loop-top source, and temperature. These differences are naturally unified by a physical picture coupling interchange and flare reconnection, offering new insights into understanding of the physical process of filament-induced jets.
comments: 10 pages, 5 figures

title: Tabular Foundation Models Dramatically Outperform Bespoke Photometric Redshift Estimators
authors: Biprateep Dey, Joshua S. Speagle
abstract: Estimating galaxy redshifts (a proxy for distance) from imaging data alone, also known as photometric redshifts (photo-$z$'s), is essential for studies of extragalactic astrophysics and cosmology. However, data-driven estimators rely on spectroscopic training datasets, which are scarce and systematically biased toward bright and easily observed galaxies. In this work, we show that tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose synthetic pretraining amounts to a learned prior over regression problems, can outperform bespoke estimators using only in-context learning. Evaluating on a widely used benchmark dataset, we find that TFMs predicting full probability distributions in a single forward pass systematically outperform bespoke estimators across both representative and biased training data regimes, matching or exceeding baselines trained on over $40{,}000$ galaxies with just $1{,}000$ training context examples. We also show that the TFM advantage is largest when little to no calibration data are available, and that it persists even when the bespoke baselines are supplemented with up to $10{,}000$ representative calibration spectra. This shows that TFMs offer a sample-efficient framework for upcoming imaging-only astronomical surveys, where observational selection bias can be mitigated simply by including a small representative calibration sample in context.
comments: Accepted for 9th Workshop on Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences (ML4PS 2026)

figs.cap: Performance scaling of TFMs and bespoke photo-$z$ estimators on the representative DC1 benchmark across training context sizes. Left: CDE loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\rm CDE}$, lower is better). Right: Point dispersion $\sigma_{\rm IQR}$ at distribution mode $z_{\rm peak}$ (log scale). TFMs continue to improve out to the full catalog. With just $1{,}000$ context galaxies, all three TFMs match or outperform full-catalog bespoke baselines, and by $5{,}000$ they substantially outperform all of them.

CDE loss of LimiX-2 (left) and of CMNN (middle), the strongest bespoke estimator at full biased context, across biased training ($N_{\rm train}=1{,}000$ to $35{,}011$) and representative calibration sample sizes ($N_{\rm cal}=0$ to $10{,}000$), on a shared color scale, along with their difference (right) $\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\rm CDE}=\mathcal{L}_{\rm LimiX}-\mathcal{L}_{\rm CMNN}$. Lower is better throughout. The outlined cells in the left and middle panels mark the least data given to LimiX-2 ($1{,}000$ biased galaxies and no calibration sample) and the most given to CMNN ($35{,}011$ biased galaxies and $10{,}000$ calibration galaxies), and the cell with the red border in the right panel marks where the advantage of LimiX-2 is largest ($\Delta\mathcal{L}_{\rm CDE}=-5.4$, with $1{,}000$ biased and $2{,}000$ calibration galaxies). LimiX-2 outperforms CMNN in all $35$ cells, by $3.2$ to $5.4$ units. With the least data, LimiX-2 trails CMNN with the most ($-11.74$ vs. $-12.23$), but with $1{,}000$ biased galaxies and $1{,}000$ calibration galaxies, LimiX-2 ($-13.35$) already outperforms CMNN with $35{,}011$ biased galaxies and $10{,}000$ calibration galaxies ($-12.23$).

Impact of the spectroscopic selection function on the training sample distributions compared to the representative test and calibration samples. Left: Redshift distribution showing the biased spectroscopic training sample (blue), the representative test sample (orange), and the representative calibration sample (green). Right: Distribution in the selection plane of $i$-band magnitude vs. $(g-z)$ color, where solid contours enclose 11.8%, 39.3%, 67.5%, and 86.4% of each sample’s galaxies (the two-dimensional Gaussian equivalents of $0.5\sigma$, $1\sigma$, $1.5\sigma$, and $2\sigma$). We observe that the spectroscopic selection preferentially removes faint ($i>24$) and high-redshift ($z>0.8$) galaxies, producing an unrepresentative training distribution, whereas the calibration sample closely matches the representative test population across all magnitudes and colors.

As Figure 1, but showing scaling of TFMs and bespoke photo-$z$ estimators under realistic spectroscopic selection bias as a function of training data size, evaluated on the same test set. We observe that TFMs scale steadily with training context size and outperform the bespoke estimators in both metrics at every training size, with LimiX-2 achieving the lowest CDE loss and scatter across all training sizes. In contrast, FlexZBoost, which performed well on the representative training data, does not scale well on the biased sample. All TFMs achieve better CDE loss with just $1{,}000$ training examples compared to GPz and FlexZBoost with the full data, and with $5{,}000$ training examples compared to CMNN with the full data.
As Figure 2, but comparing LimiX-2 to FlexZBoost instead of CMNN. As FlexZBoost has the highest CDE loss of the three bespoke estimators under selection, the margin here is the widest.

As Figure 2, but comparing LimiX-2 to GPz instead of CMNN. At every training set size, the relative advantage of LimiX-2 is smaller with $10{,}000$ calibration galaxies than with none, unlike with CMNN.

title: The Disk Awakens: IXPE's Sequel Observation of GS 1354-64 Suggests Changing-Look Behavior in the Steep-Power-Law State
authors: Swati Ravi, James F. Steiner, Megan Masterson, Lorenzo Marra, Philip Kaaret, Alexandra Veledina, Michal Dovciak, Adam Ingram, Fiamma Capitanio, Sudeb Ranjan Datta, Elise Egron, Javier A. Garcia, Ole Koenig, Honghui Liu, Herman L. Marshall, Guglielmo Mastroserio, Romana Mikusincova, Joey Neilsen, Edward J. R. Nathan, P.-O. Petrucci, Jakub Podgorny, Jiri Svoboda, Yuexin Zhang
abstract: After decades of only failed transitions, the black hole X-ray binary GS 1354-64 has undergone a complete outburst again. We present its first X-ray polarimetric investigation in the fading steep-power-law (SPL) state, following an earlier intermediate-state IXPE campaign during the same outburst. The 2-8 keV emission has a polarization degree (PD) of 2.3 +/- 0.2% and polarization angle (PA) of 5 +/- 3 degrees. Compared with the intermediate state, where PD=3.9 +0.3/-0.2% and PA=-2 +/-2 degrees, the broadband PD is lower while the PA remains consistent. The intermediate-state type-C quasi-periodic oscillation state has also disappeared, marking a major reconfiguration of the accretion flow. Assuming a distance of 7 kpc, the observed the intensity drop from 2.5% to 1.6% of the Eddington luminosity over 10.2 days is punctuated by several broad hour-to-day-scale troughs, tracing two distinct tracks in hardness-intensity space. Simultaneous spectroscopy shows the troughs' spectra contains a cooler disk with smaller apparent normalization, while no change in the Compton component's photon index or normalization is required between tracks. The model-independent analysis identifies a steeper increase in PD with energy outside the troughs, yielding G_E=1.5 +/- 0.2%/keV, compared with G_E=0.7 +0.3/-0.5%/keV during the troughs. Their duration and spectropolarimetric morphology distinguish the troughs from traditional short absorption dips seen in X-ray binaries, providing a possible stellar-mass analog of the recurrent accretion changes that drive "changing-look" behavior in supermassive black hole systems.
comments: 23 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to ApJ

title: The origin of UV emission in extremely low-mass satellite galaxies: Insights from Leo T
authors: S Amrutha, Mousumi Das, Daniel Vaz, Jarle Brinchmann
abstract: Leo T, a Milky Way (MW) satellite, is the lowest-mass gas-rich galaxy known to show recent star formation, making it an excellent laboratory for investigating star formation in the ultraviolet (UV) regime within a low-density, metal-poor environment. We present a far-UV (FUV) study using Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) data, aiming to characterize FUV star-forming clusters (SFCs), identify FUV-emitting stars, constrain their properties, and explore star formation in an extremely low-mass, metal-poor galaxy. We examined the galaxy's FUV extent and compared it with the H I distribution. We extracted thirty SFCs and derived their properties, including area, luminosity, and star formation rate (SFR), and compared them with previous studies. FUV-emitting stars and their stellar parameters were identified through cross-matching with catalogs from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE). We also estimated the global SFR and star formation efficiencies (SFEs) associated with previously identified CO clouds. The FUV luminosities of the SFCs confirm the absence of massive O and B-type stars in Leo T. The FUV-emitting stellar population consists of main-sequence (MS) stars, blue loop (BL) stars, horizontal branch stars, and emission-line (EM) stars. The upper MS and EM stars are concentrated near the optical center, whereas the lower MS and BL stars are more spatially extended. We find that five out of the six FUV-emitting stars with MUSE spectroscopy are extremely metal-poor ([Fe/H] $\leq$ -3). The (NUV - r) color profile indicates that the UV emission is dominated by stellar populations younger than 1 Gyr out to a radius $\lt$ 185 pc. Despite the recent detection of CO(1-0) emission, no SFCs are associated with the molecular clouds, which exhibit extremely low SFEs. The spatial distribution of the SFCs suggests a directional interaction with the MW.
comments: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Probing Multi-formation Channels of Dark Matter-Deficient Galaxies in a Simulated Universe
authors: Sanghyeon Han, Ho Seong Hwang, Jaehyun Lee
abstract: We investigate the formation and evolution of dark matter-deficient galaxies (DMDGs) using the IllustrisTNG100 cosmological hydrodynamical simulation. We define DMDGs as systems with a dark matter-to-stellar mass ratio below unity, and find two formation channels. In the first, galaxies that initially form within massive dark matter halos lose the majority of their dark matter and transition into DMDGs (acquired DMDGs). In the second, galaxies form with little or no dark matter from the beginning (inborn DMDGs). The two populations show distinct physical properties. Acquired DMDGs exhibit significant temporal variations in mass content, size, and kinematics, whereas inborn DMDGs show mild evolution. The former population tends to form closer to their nearest neighbor galaxies in large-scale overdense regions than the latter population does. We find that most stars in the inborn DMDGs form in situ. Their precursor gas is already metal-enriched and associated with other galaxies before formation. Tidal interactions and filamentary gas flows may contribute to the assembly of compact gas clumps, suggesting multiple formation pathways for inborn DMDGs. Our findings support the idea that there are at least two distinct channels to make galaxies dark matter deficient, which is important for understanding the formation mechanisms of these extreme systems.
comments: 28 pages, 21 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ

title: Cosmic birefringence tomography with radio galaxies I: Testing birefringence solutions to the CMB-BAO tension
authors: Toshiya Namikawa, Fumihiro Naokawa, Richard Battye, Salvatore Samuele Sirletti
abstract: We present an independent test of cosmic birefringence induced by axionlike particles (ALPs) at low redshift using radio galaxies. We focus on models that can alleviate the mild tension between recent baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements and observations of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This tension can be explained by a large cosmic birefringence rotation angle generated during the reionization epoch. Such a large rotation can arise if the recent isotropic cosmic birefringence measurements are subject to an $n\pi$ phase ambiguity, with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, or if cold dark matter injects energy into ALPs. We constrain these two scenarios by fitting the cosmic birefringence angles estimated from the jet morphologies and polarization angles of radio galaxies obtained by Battye, Jackson & Browne (2026). For the $n\pi$ model, the radio-galaxy data exclude $|n|\geq 1$ at more than $2\sigma$ for $\log_{10}(m_{\phi}/{\rm eV})\lesssim -30.7$. For the energy injection model, the data are consistent with no energy injection, but with a slight relative preference for a nonzero energy injection compared to the no-injection case. Since our samples are limited to $\sim 3000$ and there could still be several astrophysical uncertainties and statistical fluctuations, further exploration of tomographic cosmic birefringence using a large number of low-redshift radio galaxies is important for independent tests of cosmic birefringence.
comments: 10 pages, 8 figures

figs.cap: Cosmic birefringence angle as a function of redshift for specific cases of the logarithmic ALP masses, $\log_{10}(m_{\phi}/{\rm eV})$, for the $n\pi$ and energy-injection models. For the $n\pi$ model, we assume $n=1$ for all cases. If $n=0$ with the same masses, the birefringence angle at $z\leq 3$ is much smaller than $0.3^{\circ}$ and is almost overlapped with the $\beta=0^{\circ}$ horizontal line in the figure. For the energy-injection model, we assume the rescaled energy injection efficiency, $\tilde{\xi}=10$, and the start and end of the energy injection period in redshift, $z_{\rm start}=60$ and $z_{\rm end}=50$.

title: Cosmological axion-photon interactions with a nonminimal dark gauge sector
authors: Hao Jiao, Dong-Won Jung, Nils A. Nilsson
abstract: We study the cosmological evolution of radiation and dark radiation with nonminimal axion-photon-dark photon couplings. The Chern-Simons-type axion-gauge field interactions between the dark and visible sectors can induce energy conversion between photons and dark photons as well as polarization rotation during the propagation of radiation, leading to CMB spectral distortions and cosmic birefringence. Using the observed CMB monopole spectrum, we constrain the photon-dark photon energy conversion fraction, which is determined by the coupling constants and the evolution of the axion field. We further show that the parity-odd mixing interaction $\phi F\tilde{B}$ can partially relax the constraints on the standard axion-photon coupling, $\phi F\tilde{F}$, derived from the current observational limits of the cosmic birefringence angle.
comments: 24 pages, 6 figures

title: A deep learning approach to member identification and mass estimation in galaxy clusters
authors: Zicheng Wang, Liping Fu, Wei Du, Wentao Luo, Wenxiang Pei, Zhu Chen, Zhijian Luo, Yicheng Li, Jiachen Qiu, Haoran Zhao, Kaiwen Mai, Weiming Ren
abstract: Accurate dynamical mass estimates of galaxy clusters are essential for studies of cluster formation and evolution and for cosmological applications. However, interloper galaxies, which are not gravitationally bound to the cluster but are incorrectly identified as members, can bias dynamical mass measurements and increase uncertainties. We developed a probabilistic deep-learning framework for cluster member identification and dynamical mass estimation and tested sensitivity to cluster miscentring and radially dependent incompleteness in controlled mock experiments. We used mock galaxy cluster catalogues to train a two-stage model. A long short-term memory (LSTM) network assigns membership probabilities to galaxies arranged by projected phase-space proximity. These probabilities construct membership-weighted projected phase-space density maps, from which a Bayesian neural network (BNN) infers cluster masses and predictive uncertainties. The LSTM membership probabilities are well calibrated and form an isoprobability envelope in projected phase space, with the $\langle p_{\rm mem}\rangle = 0.5$ contour broadly tracing the empirical member--interloper transition. A threshold of $p_{\rm th} = 0.5$ balances member completeness and purity, with high completeness within $R_{\rm proj} < r_{200}$. Membership weighting lowers the residual scatter of the fiducial BNN mass estimator, $\mathrm{BNN}^{\mathrm{Mem}}_{\mathrm{2D}}$, to $\sigma_\epsilon = 0.120$, a 19.5% reduction relative to the unweighted baseline, although predictive uncertainties are not uniformly calibrated across BNN models. Using the brightest cluster galaxy rather than the gravitational centre lowers the median inferred mass by up to 47.6%, with larger reductions at larger centring offsets. By contrast, removing 40% of eligible non-central galaxies within $r_{200}$ lowers it by 6.1% relative to complete catalogues.
comments: 16 pages, 13 figures, 5 tables. Accepted by Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Low-variance renoising for weak gravitational lensing shear estimation
authors: Xiangchong Li
abstract: The "renoising" noise-bias correction used by Metacalibration and AnaCal adds to every galaxy image an independent noise field with the statistics of the original noise rotated by 90 degrees. The rotated field cancels, to first order in shear, the anisotropy that the shear-response operation induces in the original noise, at the cost of doubling the noise variance. We derive the general condition that an added noise field must satisfy for this cancellation: the distribution of the total noise -- the original noise transformed with the pixel shear-response operator, plus the added noise carrying an assigned shear dependence that we are free to choose -- must be independent of shear to first order. Under this condition the shear response of the renoised ellipticity is estimated from the known realization of the added noise alone. The rotated noise field, which we call rotation renoising, is one solution of the condition and yields the analytical response estimator of AnaCal. We then construct a second solution, spectral renoising, which adds only a small fraction of the original noise variance: for homogeneous Gaussian noise the added field is an independent, scaled-down copy of the image noise, and its assigned shear response is the same field passed through a fixed filter set by the noise power spectrum deconvolved by the point spread function. Image simulations show that spectral renoising keeps the multiplicative shear bias at the $10^{-3}$ level and raises the effective galaxy number density by about 20 per cent at the faint end.
comments: 18 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables

title: Cosmological constraints on extra radiation and early dark energy with lepton asymmetry and varying quark masses
authors: Yo Toda
abstract: We investigate cosmological constraints on extra radiation and axionlike early dark energy (EDE), allowing primordial lepton asymmetry or light-quark-mass variation during big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN). We combine Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae, and primordial helium and deuterium measurements. When both extra radiation and lepton asymmetry are allowed, we obtain $N_{\rm eff}=3.27\pm0.16$, $\xi=0.017\pm0.011$, and $H_0=69.24\pm0.92\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. A positive lepton asymmetry compensates the helium increase caused by extra radiation, allowing a higher inferred Hubble constant even with the LBT helium measurement, which agrees with standard BBN. For EDE, primordial-abundance measurements instead restrict the higher baryon densities associated with larger EDE fractions, which reduce the predicted deuterium abundance. Allowing lepton asymmetry does not relax this restriction. In contrast, a positive light-quark-mass variation increases deuterium and compensates this reduction, permitting larger EDE fractions and a higher inferred Hubble constant. The same variation leaves the extra-radiation constraint nearly unchanged. We also find that allowing lepton asymmetry relaxes the 95\% upper limit on the summed neutrino mass from $0.0640\,{\rm eV}$ to $0.0777\,{\rm eV}$ in the extra-radiation model.
comments: 16 pages, 5 figures

title: Efficient GLS map-making and assessment of $1/f$ noise impact for future CMB satellite missions
authors: Marta Monelli, Guillaume Patanchon, Avinash Anand
abstract: Time-correlated $1/f$ noise is a major source of large-scale contamination in measurements of the polarized cosmic microwave background (CMB) that can limit sensitivity to primordial $B$ modes. Generalized least-squares (GLS) map-making is optimal for stationary Gaussian noise when its covariance is known, but practical implementations rely on approximations to make the computation tractable. In particular, approximating the noise covariance as circulant enables efficient map-making using fast Fourier transform, but introduces artificial edge effects when applied to finite data chunks. We introduce STITCH (STatistical Inpainting for Timeline CHunks), a preprocessing method that mitigates these effects by extending time-ordered data chunks with synthetic samples that make the extended timelines statistically consistent with the assumed circulant noise model. They can then be processed with standard circulant GLS solvers, preserving their computational efficiency while reducing residuals associated with chunk boundaries. Simulations show that STITCH substantially suppresses these edge effects, bringing the resulting noise power spectra close to those obtained when the circulant approximation holds. We demonstrate negligible impact of our procedure on the recovered signal, such as $E\to B$ leakage, even at large scales. Finally, we investigate how temporal $1/f$ noise projects onto angular scales for representative LiteBIRD-, \emph{Planck}-, and PICO-like scanning strategies. Using noise simulations spanning a range of temporal noise parameters, we fit an effective model to the resulting angular noise spectra. These results provide an empirical characterization of the temporal-to-angular noise mapping for the configurations studied and a basis for further investigations of correlated noise in future CMB polarization missions.
comments: 25 pages + appendix and bibliography, 17 figures, 4 tables

title: The Pointing Error Due To Laser Propagation in Space Plasma for TianQin Gravitational Wave Detection
authors: S.W. Zhou, W. Su, S.Y. Zhou, C.F. Li, J.X Zhang
abstract: TianQin, a space-borne gravitational wave observatory, is designed to detect gravitational-wave signals via laser interferometry. As the inhomogeneous space plasma surrounds the inter-satellite laser links, the propagation of the laser in space plasma can introduce pointing error noise. In this work, we quantitatively assess the effect of plasma on the pointing accuracy of TQ's inter-satellite laser links. We employ a magnetohydrodynamic model to simulate the plasma distribution around the TQ orbit for different orbital orientations. Using the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method to conduct the ray-tracing calculations over a TQ orbital cycle under a solar wind dynamic pressure close to the 23-year average, we find that the plasma-induced laser deflection angle and pointing eccentricity are on the order of $10^{-20} \ \mathrm{rad}$ and picometers, respectively. These values are significantly lower than TQ's requirements. Our results demonstrate that the impact of space plasma on TQ's pointing error is negligible in moderate space weather conditions, indicating a positive outlook for the TQ mission.
comments: 14 pages, 7 figures Published in Space Weather

title: The Peculiar Astrometric Behaviour and Radio Structure of the Quasar 1524-136 Revealed with Very Long Baseline Interferometry
authors: Angelina Osetrova, Sándor Frey, Oleg Titov, Alexey Melnikov, Panna Gelle
abstract: According to astrometric very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations accurate to sub-milliarcsecond levels, the radio quasar 1524-136 (J1526-1351) exhibited an exceptionally large shift, more than 0.1", between the 1990s and 2010s. This luminous quasar is known for its extended (~0.4"), highly asymmetric and non-collinear jet structure. Here we analyse historical VLBI astrometric and imaging data, as well as Gaia optical astrometric information, to find the cause of the sudden apparent change in the position. At the X band (~8.4 GHz frequency), where radio positions are conventionally measured, the core region brightened substantially relative to the hotspot at the end of the northern jet. As a result, the brightness peak shifted from the hotspot to the core, causing the VLBI position to shift accordingly. Similar changes could affect the astrometric positions of other radio sources. A better understanding of the astrophysical reasons behind them is important for maintaining the stability of the VLBI-based celestial reference frame.
comments: 22 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in the journal Symmetry

title: Hoag-type Galaxies: A Photometric Study of the Cores and Rings of Thirty Systems from the DESI Legacy Survey
authors: Jingshuo Yang, Cheng Li
abstract: Hoag-type galaxies contain a smooth central core surrounded by a detached outer ring, but their rarity has limited previous studies mainly to individual systems. We identify thirty galaxies with apparent Hoag-type morphology in DESI imaging by visually inspecting two machine-learning ring-galaxy catalogues and analyse their core and ring properties using DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys $g$, $r$, and $z$ images. We measure the rings after subtracting two-dimensional core models and compare the cores with matched SDSS galaxies. The cores lie predominantly on the red sequence, whereas the rings span a broader colour range extending toward the blue cloud. The cores broadly follow early-type mass scaling relations, but their mass-matched distributions tend towards slightly bluer colours, smaller sizes, higher stellar-mass surface densities, and lower concentrations and Sérsic indices. Of the 16 systems with SDSS group information, 14 (87.5 per cent) are centrals, compared with $\sim64\%$ in the mass-matched early-type control sample. The halo-mass and large-scale overdensity distributions become much more similar after central--satellite status is also matched. Ring stellar-mass surface density and normalized width decrease with increasing core-plus-inner-halo to ring mass ratio. Most core $R_{90}$ values lie inside the outermost stable circular orbit of a simplified core-plus-ring model, while the rings frequently extend across its unstable interval. The slightly bluer core colours, lower concentrations, and lower Sérsic indices suggest a possible secular contribution, but the compact, dense cores imply more complex structural assembly than a simple diffuse-pseudobulge origin. The high central fraction may favour gas retention and ring survival by reducing satellite-specific environmental processing. The diversity of ring properties nevertheless leaves room for multiple formation pathways.
comments: 19 pages, 15 figures (9 in the main text and 6 in the appendix)

title: Optical clock network tracks tidal variations of the gravity potential
authors: Kilian Stahl, Ingo Nosske, Chetan Vishwakarma, Tim Lücke, Joshua Klose, Erik Benkler, Alexander Kuhl, Shambo Mukherjee, Thomas Legero, Jochen Kronjäger, Uwe Sterr, Christian Lisdat, Sören Dörscher, Chen-Hao Feng, Matthew Y. H. Johnson, Jacques-Olivier Gaudron, Wei Huang, Jacob Tunesi, Xi Zhang, Marco Schioppo, Adam L. Parke, Ian R. Hill, Heiner Denker, Biplab Dutta, Etienne Cantin, Olivier Lopez, Anne Amy-Klein, Christian Chardonnet, Benjamin Pointard, Rodolphe Le Targat, Jérôme Lodewyck, Paul-Eric Pottie, Ichiro Ushijima, Masao Takamoto, Hidetoshi Katori, Yogeshwar B. Kale, Stefano Condio, Irene Goti, Tommaso Petrucciani, Cecilia Clivati, Simone Donadello, Filippo Levi, Davide Calonico, Marco Pizzocaro
abstract: Gravity affects the passage of time, as described by General Relativity. On Earth, the rate of a clock as seen by a fixed observer changes by about one part in $10^{16}$ per metre in height. Chronometric levelling exploits this effect to directly measure differences in gravity potential by comparing distant clocks. It has been proposed as a complementary approach to established geodetic techniques for linking height reference systems and monitoring the terrestrial gravity potential. Experimental demonstrations have to date focused primarily on static potential differences. Yet, the potentials of the Moon, the Sun and other celestial bodies as well as the Earth's response to their tidal forcing change clock rates by several $10^{-17}$, providing a predictable test signal to demonstrate optical clock networks resolving small variations in relativistic time dilation. Here, we report chronometric observations of time-varying gravity potential differences using a network of optical clocks and phase-stabilized fibre links in Europe. Two distinct geographical configurations, with baselines of about 800 km each, result in different combinations of diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components. One comparison uses a transportable optical clock as a remote sensor. The measured rate shifts track the tidal variations, resolving the predicted signal within 1 d of measurement and agreeing with model predictions. These results extend experimental chronometric levelling from static to dynamic potential differences and highlight the need to account for the time dependence of relativistic time dilation in frequency metrology. They also open the prospect for quantum clock networks with improved stability and availability to move beyond known tides and monitor other gravity potential variations, such as those arising from surface deformation and mass redistribution in geologically or volcanically active regions.

title: Detection of HNCOH+ in the interstellar medium
authors: M. Rey-Montejo, I. Jimenez-Serra, M. Sanz-Novo, V. Lattanzi, S. Thorwirth, V. M. Rivilla, S. Zeng, L. Colzi, D. San Andres, A. Megias, A. Martinez-Henares, M. A. Requena-Torres, S. Martin, B. Tercero, P. de Vicente
abstract: Only five out of the $\sim$350 molecules detected in the interstellar medium (ISM) carry the isocyanate functional group (NCO), the essential substructure of peptide bonds in proteins. Among them are isocyanic acid (HNCO) and its most stable N-protonated isomer H$_2$NCO$^+$. Previous studies have predicted that the O-protonated isomer HNCOH$^+$ should be present in the ISM; yet this species has remained elusive. We search for the metastable HNCOH$^+$ towards the Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027, where H$_2$NCO$^+$ has already been detected. We use an ultra-deep broadband spectral survey carried out towards G+0.693-0.027 with the Yebes 40-m, IRAM 30-m and APEX telescopes covering nearly 150 GHz of bandwidth between 31 and 275 GHz. We report the first detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM with a column density of $N$ = (9.9 $\pm$ 0.5)$\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, which corresponds to a molecular abundance relative to H$_2$ of (7.3$^{+1.3} _{-1.0}$)$\times$10$^{-11}$. With the measured H$_2$NCO$^+$ column density of $N$ = (2.6 $\pm$ 0.3) $\times 10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, this yields a HNCOH$^+$/H$_2$NCO$^+$ ratio of 3.8$^{+0.5} _{-0.4}$. This result is consistent with recent kinetic calculations that favour the formation of HNCOH$^+$ over H$_2$NCO$^+$. The detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM broadens the inventory of molecules known to contain the isocyanate functional group and reinforces recent works showing that isomer abundances in the ISM do not necessarily correlate with thermodynamic stability.
comments: Letter, Accepted in A&A

title: Towards an Astronomical Use of New-Generation Geodetic Observations
authors: Víctor Pérez-Díez
abstract: This thesis explores the astronomical use of observations from the VLBI Global Observing System (VGOS), a next-generation geodetic network designed to improve the precision of terrestrial and celestial reference frames and Earth orientation parameters. Although primarily conceived for geodesy, its wide frequency coverage and regular monitoring of compact active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable opportunities for astrophysics. We develop a calibration pipeline that transforms VGOS correlator outputs into full-polarization, calibrated visibilities suitable for astronomical imaging. The procedure combines linear-to-circular polarization conversion, instrumental phase and amplitude calibration, and a new wideband global fringe-fitting algorithm that accounts for dispersive ionospheric effects. Regularized maximum likelihood imaging is then used to reconstruct multi-frequency intensity and polarimetric images. The pipeline is applied to the blazar 1803+784 and five additional AGN: 3C418, 0059+581, 0613+570, 1849+670, and 2229+695. We measure frequency-dependent core shifts, spectral indices, and Faraday rotation properties. For 1803+784, the fitted core-shift index is $k_r = 0.73^{+0.12}_{-0.19}$, suggesting departures from a simple conical jet in energy equipartition. Finally, we apply the reconstructed source models to correct structure-dependent effects in geodetic VLBI observables. The correction reduces closure-delay scatter and post-fit residuals for strongly structured sources, particularly 3C418, while its effectiveness depends on source variability and the temporal proximity of the imaging observations. These results demonstrate the dual scientific value of VGOS as a powerful multi-frequency astronomical VLBI instrument and as a means of improving geodetic measurements.
comments: PhD thesis, Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM). Supervisors: Iván Martí-Vidal and Rafael Bachiller García. Defended on 19 October 2026. 230 pages

title: Dust growth in the early Universe: insight from the NewCluster spin-off simulation
authors: J. K. Jang, Yohan Dubois, Francisco Rodriguez Montero, San Han, Jinsu Rhee, Diana Ismail, Gyeong-Hwan Byun, Changyeon Yu, Seyoung Jeon, Sukyoung K. Yi
abstract: We investigate dust evolution in galaxies at $z\sim5$ using a spin-off run of the \NC\ cosmological zoom-in simulation with a live two-species, two-size dust model. We find that dust evolution follows three metallicity-dependent phases. At $\log(Z/Z_\odot)<-1$, dust is dominated by stellar ejecta and produces a shallow, featureless UV extinction curve whose normalized wavelength dependence is similar to that of the Calzetti attenuation law (Phase I). At $-1\leq \log(Z/Z_\odot)<-0.5$, efficient silicate accretion drives rapid dust growth, producing silicate-rich dust and SMC-like extinction curves (Phase II). At $\log(Z/Z_\odot)\geq-0.5$, carbonaceous grain growth also becomes efficient, yielding a more balanced grain mixture and Milky-Way-like extinction curves (Phase III). In addition, local dust-to-metal ratios are strongly suppressed in regions affected by recent clustered supernova feedback, further complicating the interpretation of high-$z$ observations. Despite some successes, our galaxies lie below current observationally inferred dust masses and dust-to-metal ratios for high-redshift galaxies. The resulting depletion patterns suggest that the fixed Fe-bearing olivine composition assumed in our current dust model may be too restrictive for chemically young galaxies, and that metallicity-dependent grain compositions may be required to explain the dust content of the early Universe.
comments: 15 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

title: Feeding or Fleeing: The Impact of Enhanced Early Black Hole Growth on Circumgalactic Clumps at $z > 6$
authors: Floor van Donkelaar, Lucas Tortora, Debora Sijacki
abstract: The circumgalactic medium (CGM) of massive high-redshift galaxies contains inflowing filamentary gas, recycled material, and feedback-driven outflows. We investigate the formation and evolution of dense CGM clumps in two cosmological zoom-in simulations of the same massive halo at $z > 6$: the fiducial Fable model and the modified Fable-SE model, which includes enhanced early black hole growth through mild super-Eddington accretion. We identify dense gas clumps in the CGM and follow their gas properties, stellar content, and radial evolution across cosmic time. At the resolution probed here, the two simulations show broadly similar distributions of clump gas mass, gas size and associated stellar mass. Instead, the clump populations differ mainly in their abundance, metallicity, and radial evolution. Fable-SE produces substantially more metal-enriched clumps, including an outward-moving population during the strong AGN-driven blow-out phase at $z \lesssim 7$. These systems are associated with disturbed HI-rich gas and relatively high gas densities, linking the increased prevalence of dense, metal-enriched CGM structures in Fable-SE to its stronger AGN-driven blow-out phase. Although inward migration dominates overall, Fable-SE also contains an outward-moving clump population during the blow-out phase, with some clumps moving beyond the virial radius. Our results therefore indicate that the distribution of dense CGM clumps around massive high-redshift galaxies reflects both filamentary accretion and feedback-driven CGM evolution, with strong early AGN activity associated with the outward migration of dense, metal-enriched gas structures containing relatively cool gas.
comments: Comments and suggestions welcome prior to submission to MNRAS

title: Search for Cosmic Rays in GRANDProto300
authors: Jolan Lavoisier, Aurélien Benoit-Lévy, Kumiko Kotera, Mauricio Bustamante, Marion Guelfand, Nathan Lebas, Takashi Sako, Xishui Tian, GRAND Collaboration
abstract: GRANDProto300 is a prototype array of the GRAND experiment, designed to validate the technique of autonomous radio-detection of astroparticles by detecting cosmic rays with energies between 10$^{17} - 10^{18.5}$ eV. This observation will further enable the study of the Galactic-to-extragalactic source transition region. Between November 2024 and June 2025, 46 antennas were operational, and since July 2025, 63 antennas have been collecting data stably. We present here our cosmic-ray search pipeline, that involves several filtering steps: (1) exclusion of clustered (in time and space) noise events, (2) polarization cut, (3) zenith arrival cut, and (4) delay in expected trigger cut. The efficiency is evaluated on the latest batch of data from July 2025 to October 2025. Additionally, we present an identification layer that is being developed: a CNN-based algorithm to discriminate between noise and cosmic-ray signals, using signal traces. We present the accuracy of our model, trained both on simulations and on real cosmic-ray signal datasets.
comments: Presented at the 60th Rencontres de Moriond on Very High Energy Phenomena in the Universe (Moriond VHEPU 2026). 4 pages, 1 figure

title: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) - System Design and Instrumentation
authors: Nils Heyer for the RNO-G Collaboration, Steven Barwick, AJ Nielsen
abstract: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is designed to measure cosmic neutrinos in the EeV range through an array of radio antennas detecting nanosecond-long radio flashes. In this contribution, the RNO-G electronic system is outlined, illustrating how signals are measured from the antennas to the recorded pulses. We present new instrumentation developments, focusing on electric melters to install LPDA antennas into the Greenlandic ice sheet. The new system will simplify deployment and reduce positioning uncertainty to $\pm$2cm (x/y) and $\pm$1°(rotational). We report on field tests from the RNO-G site at Summit Station.
comments: Presented at the Topical Workshop on Electronics for Particle Physics - TWEPP2026

title: Dwarf Galaxy Reticulum II's MeerKAT L-Band Observation: Constraining WIMP Dark Matter
authors: Phillip Badenhorst, Michael Sarkis, Yin-Zhe Ma, Wen-Qing Guo, Geoff Beck, Qiang Yuan, Gyula I.G. Jozsa, Steven G. Murray
abstract: The nature of dark matter remains one of the most profound open questions in modern physics, with weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) among the leading candidates proposed to account for the observed anomalies across cosmic scales. If WIMPs annihilate or decay in the dense dark matter haloes of nearby galaxies, the resulting high-energy electrons/positrons can produce synchrotron radiation in the presence of ambient magnetic fields, yielding a potentially detectable radio signature. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are particularly promising targets for indirect dark matter searches due to their high mass-to-light ratios and low astrophysical foreground contamination. While radio observations have been widely used to constrain WIMP properties in these systems, the resulting limits remain highly sensitive to poorly constrained magnetic field assumptions. Here we utilize L-band ($1.3$--$1.5$ GHz) observations from the MeerKAT array directed towards dwarf galaxy Reticulum II and measure the surface brightness profile across the dwarf galaxy. Combining these measurements with theoretical models of WIMP annihilation and yield 95% confidence level upper limits on the WIMP annihilation cross-section $\langle\sigma v\rangle \lesssim 10^{-26}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for masses $m_\chi \sim 10$-$200$ GeV (with the assumed uniform magnetic field model and diffusion constant). As next-generation radio facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array come online, robust characterisation of magnetic environments in dwarf galaxies will be essential to fully exploit their sensitivity to the particle nature of dark matter.
comments: 16 pages, 8 figures

title: Robust statistical significance for Gravitational Wave inference
authors: Alexandre Sébastien Göttel
abstract: The field of gravitational-wave data analysis heavily relies on Bayes factors to make statements about astrophysical effects in events detected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration. This is true on an event level, for example when discussing the potential detection of precession or eccentricity, as well as on a population level. For the latter, perhaps the main limiting factor is the reliance on the output from event-level nested sampling analyses, which is known to introduce growing uncertainties and biases as the number of detections increases. In both cases, while Bayes factors are useful when comparing different models, because the underlying distribution of Bayes factors in noise is unknown, it is often not possible to use them to make quantifiable statistical statements. Their statistical meaning is also questionable in the at least $20\%$ of gravitational-wave events that contain transient noise artifacts. This paper shows that it is possible to use evidence networks, which can infer Bayes factors after learning the distinguishability between datasets, to solve all of the aforementioned problems. By being able to calculate up to $10^5$ Bayes factors per second, we can construct background distributions of Bayes factors under different signal assumptions to estimate significance. We show that the high precision achieved allows us to scale the results from up to $10^4$ events with no discernable bias on population-level quantities, while laying the foundations for a likelihood-free method that does not rely on the assumption of Gaussian and stationary noise.
comments: 9 pages including bibliography, 6 figures

title: The stellar orbit distribution of 24 late-type galaxies observed by MUSE
authors: Le Zhang, Ling Zhu, Jesús Falcon-Barroso
abstract: We selected 24 nearby late-type galaxies from the MUSE archive with kinematic coverage extending to at least one effective radius. Stellar kinematics were extracted with the GIST pipeline using pPXF, and axisymmetric Schwarzschild models were constructed with \textsc{dynamite}. The stellar orbits of each galaxy were classified by circularity into dynamically cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating components, and we calculated the corresponding luminosity fractions of each component within $R_{\mathrm{e}}$. Our results confirm the mass-dependent trends in orbital structure previously identified from CALIFA galaxies and reproduced by IllustrisTNG. We further checked the morphology of each component and calculated the edge-on flattening of the cold, warm, and hot+CR components. With the high-quality MUSE data, we find that the dynamically warm components are common in low-mass late-type spiral galaxies, suggesting that their discs are dynamically warmer and vertically thicker than those of more massive spirals. We regard this as a tentative result, given the limited sample size.

title: RAKI: High-Order Alternative Finite Differences for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics
authors: Rahime Matur, Beyhan Karakas, Ian Hawke, Nils Andersson
abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) and black hole--neutron star mergers are among the most important multimessenger sources. Observations of these events could provide valuable insights into several unresolved phenomena, ranging from the efficiency of magnetic field amplification during and after mergers to the formation of magnetars and jets. Understanding these phenomena requires accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution, which remains a challenge for state-of-the-art general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations. In this work, we present \texttt{RAKI} (Relativistic Astrophysics Code Implementation of the Alternative Finite Difference Approach for GRMHD), the first GRMHD code to simulate BNS mergers using high-order alternative finite-difference methods with adaptive-order WENO (AFD-WENO-AO) reconstruction and a fully non-staggered, node-centred vector-potential formulation. The code achieves up to ninth-order convergence in smooth test problems while accurately capturing discontinuities. In magnetised Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) star tests, \texttt{RAKI} retains $99.2$ per cent of the initial maximum magnetic field strength over ${\sim}2$ ms, exhibiting an order of magnitude less magnetic field loss than a reference GRMHD code at the same resolution. In BNS merger simulations, fifth-order AFD-WENO-AO reconstruction yields approximately third-order convergence of the gravitational-wave phase in both magnetised and unmagnetised models. The discrete no-monopole constraint is preserved to machine precision without staggered grids, even during BNS mergers with moving refinement regions. These results establish \texttt{RAKI} as a high-order, non-staggered GRMHD framework for accurate modelling of magnetic field evolution in neutron star mergers and its implications for multimessenger astrophysics.
comments: 21 pages, 12 figures, 1 table

figs.cap: Convergence of the third-, fifth-, seventh-, and ninth-order AFD-WENO-AO schemes for the circularly polarised Alfvén wave test at $t=2$. The errors are measured using the $L_{2}$ norm of $B^{y}$ relative to the analytic solution. All simulations employ $N_{x}=16,32,64,$ and $128$, with an additional $N_{x}=96$ for the ninth-order scheme and $N_{y}=N_{z}=8$ throughout. The third-, fifth-, and seventh-order schemes achieve their expected convergence rates, while the ninth-order scheme exhibits ninth-order convergence up to $N_{x}=64$ points. Beyond this resolution, the convergence rate worsens when using the RK4 time integrator but recovers the expected ninth-order accuracy with RK87.

Balsara1 and Balsara3 are shown at $t=0.4$, while Balsara5 is shown at $t=0.55$.

title: The first mass peak of merging black holes from core binding energies and jet-driven explosions
authors: Nikki Yat Ning Wang, Dmitry Shishkin, Noam Soker
abstract: We show that the jittering-jets explosion mechanism (JJEM) can qualitatively reproduce the shape of the black hole (BH) mass distribution observed by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA and quantitatively reproduce the peak around $M_{p1} \simeq 10 M_\odot$. To show this, we construct a toy model that captures the JJEM physics that explodes all massive stars, even when BHs form. According to the JJEM, BHs form when the star's binding energy is large, implying a massive progenitor with initial mass $M_i \gtrsim 25 M_\odot$, and when jets are launched along a fixed axis, implying a rapidly rotating pre-collapse stellar core. In this case, the jets are launched along the core's angular momentum and are inefficient at removing mass near the equatorial plane; when the stellar binding energy is large, a large fraction of the equatorial mass is accreted to form the BH. The toy model includes two parameters: the threshold binding energy in the core for BH formation and the jet opening angle along the poles. Although our finding is encouraging for the JJEM, future hydrodynamical simulations must determine the exact condition for BH formation in the JJEM and the BH mass.
comments: Will submit to PASP in two days to allow for comments; 11 pages, 5 figures

title: Tidal disruption or plunge: the role of neutron star internal structure in black hole-neutron star mergers
authors: Yatharth Chaurasiya, Ritam Mallick
abstract: The outcome of black hole--neutron star (BHNS) mergers is studied using a general-relativistic mass-shedding condition in the Kerr spacetime, which determines the tidal-disruption radius from the mass ratio, the black hole (BH) spin, the neutron star (NS) compactness, and the ratio of central to average density, $\eta=\frac{\rho_{c}}{\bar\rho}$. Comparing this radius with the innermost stable circular orbit, we map the boundary between tidal disruption and plunge for two relativistic mean-field equations of state (EOSs) and for an ensemble of about $10^4$ agnostic EOSs spanning the current uncertainty in the NS radius. We find that the disruption threshold is set mainly by the compactness, but NSs with the same compactness and different $\eta$ can have different outcomes. Using the tidal disruption radius, we construct a remnant-mass model calibrated against 70 numerical-relativity simulations, which reproduces the remnant mass with an accuracy comparable to existing fits. Applying the disruption criterion and the remnant model to GW200105, GW200115, and the candidate BHNS event GW230529, we find that GW200105 and GW200115 are consistent with a direct plunge. GW230529 lies close to the disruption threshold and may have undergone marginal disruption, leaving only a low-mass remnant.
comments: 15 pages, 6 figures

title: VERITAS Limits on Dark Matter Annihilation in the Galactic Center Halo
authors: A. Archer, P. Bangale, J. T. Bartkoske, W. Benbow, N. R. Bond, J. H. Buckley, Y. Chen, J. L. Christiansen, A. J. Chromey, A. Duerr, M. Errando, M. Escobar Godoy, J. Escudero Pedrosa, S. Feldman, Q. Feng, S. Filbert, L. Fortson, A. Furniss, W. Hanlon, O. Hervet, C. E. Hinrichs, J. Holder, D. Huang, T. B. Humensky, M. Iskakova, W. Jin, E. Joshi, M. Kertzman, M. Kherlakian, D. Ragan, P. T. Reynolds, E. Roache, J. L. Ryan, I. Sadeh, L. Saha, H. Salzmann, M. Santander, G. H. Sembroski, D. Tak, J. V. Tucci, V. V. Vassiliev, D. A. Williams, S. L. Wong, T. Yoshikoshi
abstract: Well-motivated models of particle dark matter predict its self-annihilation into Standard Model end states, which may be detected by particle detectors or telescopes. We conduct an indirect dark matter search using gamma rays detected by the VERITAS telescope from within $2^\circ$ of the Galactic Center. A template-based approach is used for background estimation, increasing our sensitivity to sources of gamma-ray emission with spatial extents comparable to the $3.5^\circ$ VERITAS field of view. The analysis benefits from data taken exclusively at large zenith angles, which results in an increased effective area at energies above ~1 TeV, compared to small zenith angle observations. No significant gamma-ray signal is observed in the search region, resulting in upper limits on the end-state-dependent dark matter annihilation cross sections. Cross sections as low as $\langle \sigma_\text{ann} v\rangle = 1.77\times 10^{-25} \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$ are excluded at 95% confidence assuming complete annihilation into $\tau^+ \tau^-$, an Einasto profile, and a dark matter mass of 1 TeV.

title: Energy-Dependent Hard X-Ray QPP Modulation in M- and X-Class Solar Flares Observed by Aditya-L1/HEL1OS
authors: Sachin Rajkapoor Kanaujiya, Ram Ajor Maurya, Valery M. Nakariakov
abstract: Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in solar-flare hard X-ray (HXR) emission provide observational constraints on the temporal variability of flare energy release and energetic-electron production. In our previous study, we established a systematic catalogue of HXR QPPs in HEL1OS observations of X-class solar flares, identifying statistically significant pulsations in 25 of 34 events with sufficient data quality (S. Rajkapoor Kanaujiya et al. 2026). Here, we extend this investigation by comparing the energy dependence of the modulation depth of QPPs in M- and X-class flares across four HEL1OS energy channels spanning 8-20 keV. The comparison comprises 18 M-class events and the X-class sample from our previous study, with the number of available measurements varying between energy channels. In both flare populations, the modulation depth increases with photon energy. For M-class flares, it rises from approximately 2.3% at 8-11 keV to 13.2% at 17-20 keV, whereas for X-class flares increase from approximately 1.0% to 3.1%. The stronger increase towards higher energies in the M-class sample constitutes the principal observational contrast. These results demonstrate an energy-dependent increase in the relative amplitude of HXR QPPs in both populations and motivate a systematic statistical assessment of whether their energy-dependent modulation-depth distributions differ. The comparison provides a basis for constraining models of QPP generation and the modulation of energetic-electron emission during solar flares.

Blue solid curves and square markers represent the M-class sample, whereas red dashed curves and circular markers represent the X-class sample. Faint lines show the modulation-depth measurements for individual flares. The annotations indicate the number of events contributing to each energy-channel distribution. The two statistical representations provide complementary views of the central tendency and dispersion of the measurements, while the energy-dependent sample sizes should be considered when interpreting differences between flare classes.

title: A MUSE and MeerKAT study of dynamics and star formation in HCG 16
authors: Ixaka Labadie-García, Enrique Pérez, Julián Garrido, Roger Ianjamasimanana, Lourdes Verdes-Montenegro
abstract: Context. Hickson Compact Groups (HCGs) present an ideal environment for studying galaxy interactions. HCG 16 is a group of five galaxies in an intermediate stage of evolution (Phase 2), with several members displaying signs of interaction, including distorted morphologies, tidal features, and enhanced star formation rates. Aims. We aim to better understand the evolution of HCG 16 and its member galaxies, focusing on the relationship between neutral hydrogen and star formation, while reconstructing the interaction history of the group. Methods. We analysed MUSE data processed with pyPipe3D to extract H$\alpha$ images and stellar population synthesis results, and reduced MeerKAT data to produce a high-resolution HI cube. We examined the structure and dynamics of the H$\alpha$ and HI lines in both 2D and 3D, and produced spatially resolved star formation histories to compare the inner and outer parts of the galaxies. Results. We identify a major star formation episode in HCG 16 beginning ~400-500 Myr ago, coinciding with the passage of NGC 848 close to the other member galaxies, and that continued at least until 50-60 Myr ago in some galaxies. The HI distribution is highly perturbed in the group, although HCG 16a retains a nearly regular disk, while HCG 16b has associated H$\alpha$ tails. Conclusions. The passage of NGC 848 probably activated star formation in HCG 16, but cannot by itself explain the current starburst activity in HCG 16c and 16d. The evolution of the group is better explained by multiple interactions among its members than by a single strong encounter.

title: Preparation of a celestial field for precise VLBI observations of the JUICE spacecraft: a test case of the Venus flyby
authors: Krisztina Perger, Sándor Frey, Giuseppe Cimò, Dominic Dirkx, Jasper Edwards, Sam Fayolle, Judit Fogasy, Krisztina É. Gabányi, Leonid I. Gurvits, Máté Krezinger, Guifré Molera Calvés, Vidhya Pallichadath, Noor Masdiana Md Said, Bert Vermeersen
abstract: The Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer mission, launched in 2023, is on its way to the Jovian system, to arrive in 2031. The Planetary Radio Interferometry and Doppler Experiment performs radio astronomical observations of the spacecraft already in its interplanetary cruise phase. Since the sky density of potential compact radio sources suitable as phase-reference calibrators in very long baseline interferometry observations is low, densifying the celestial reference frame along the Ecliptic is an essential task in support of JUICE. In preparation for the JUICE gravity assist manoeuvre at Venus in August 2025, to support the accurate reconstruction of the spacecraft state vector, we selected in-beam calibrator source candidates along the JUICE trajectory. Additionally, we attempted to link known nearby bright compact reference sources from the Radio Fundamental Catalog to the International Celestial Reference Frame. We performed nodding-style phase-referencing VLBI observations with the European VLBI Network at 8.4GHz, targeting nine in-beam calibrator candidate and three RFC sources in the celestial vicinity of JUICE's trajectory during its Venus flyby. We linked their positions to nearby ICRF sources by means of relative astrometry. Four of the ICC targets and all RFC sources were detected and imaged with the EVN, and their coordinates determined with typically sub-mas precision. Although none of the targeted ICC sources proved suitable as VLBI phase-reference calibrators because of being too faint or resolved, their newly-determined positions and flux densities could in principle be used to verify the detection of the spacecraft at the time of the actual flyby around Venus. During the detailed analysis of the ICC targets, we found that the structure of one of them, J0843+1826 is resolved on mas scale, and the other one, J0843+1814 is a young radio galaxy, likely a member of a cluster.

title: Recent advances in numerical modeling of solar inertial modes
authors: Yuto Bekki, Laurent Gizon
abstract: Inertial modes are low-frequency global oscillations in rotating fluids, restored by the Coriolis force. Long-term observations of horizontal flows on the solar surface have led to the detection of various inertial modes on the Sun, opening a new window into the structure and dynamics of the solar interior. Here, we focus on recent advances in the theoretical modeling of solar inertial modes within a purely hydrodynamic framework, leaving magnetohydrodynamic effects beyond the scope of this review. Because the low-frequency oscillations of a differentially rotating spherical shell depend sensitively on the rotation profile and the properties of the medium, they are primarily studied using numerical models. We first summarize how linear eigenmode analyses have enabled the identification and classification of different families of inertial modes observed on the Sun, and how these models reveal the strong diagnostic potential of inertial modes for probing poorly constrained parameters in the deep convection zone, such as turbulent viscosity and superadiabaticity. The amplitudes of linearly stable modes can be estimated from their response to stochastic forcing, whereas those of linearly unstable modes must be determined using nonlinear numerical modeling. We further discuss the possible dynamical roles of large-amplitude inertial modes in transporting heat and angular momentum in the Sun. By clarifying what has been established and what remains uncertain, this review provides a framework for interpreting current observations and guiding future theoretical developments in this rapidly evolving field.
comments: 28 pages, 7 figures; Accepted for publication in Solar Physics

title: Mapping cluster angular momentum with the rotational kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect
authors: Jack Y. L. Kwok, Bernardita Ried Guachalla, William R. Coulton, Selim C. Hotinli, Emmanuel Schaan
abstract: Galaxy clusters carry angular momentum. If the intracluster gas rotates coherently, the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) effect imprints a dipole on the microwave sky centered on the cluster. We show that microwave maps alone can be used to reconstruct a noisy vector field tracing the projected angular momentum of the ionized gas. We present an optimal multifrequency matched filter (MMF) that isolates the rotational kSZ (rkSZ) signal from the much larger miscentered thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect, cosmic microwave, and infrared background contributions, improving on both real-space oriented stacking and matched filtering of maps cleaned with full-sky multifrequency weights. For the rkSZ profile, we introduce a simple model for coherent intracluster gas rotation and validate it against TNG-Cluster and TNG300-1. The model consists of differentially rotating concentric shells with constant equatorial tangential velocity, characterized by a mass- and redshift-indepedent tangential-to-circular velocity ratio of $v_{\rm tan}/V_{c,200c}=0.18$. Using this model, we forecast single-cluster signal-to-noise (SNR) as a function of mass and redshift for Simons Observatory; cross-correlation with an external catalog of rotation proxies yields a cumulative detection SNR. For an idealized mass-limited catalog with perfectly known spin directions, the cumulative SNR of our optimal MMF reaches $\approx 53$, $25$, and $6$ when including all clusters above $\log_{10}(M_{200c}/M_\odot)>14$, 14.5, and 15, respectively. This work provides a practical framework for CMB measurements of intracluster gas rotation, with applications to the rotational contribution to non-thermal pressure in cluster mass calibration, as well as spin alignments and clustering biases.
comments: 26 pages, 15 figures

The shaded region denotes the 16th-84th percentile across clusters, and the colored line denotes the median. While the simple estimate obtain an amplitude that agree with simulation for all considered mass and redshift, it cannot explain the radial features in the tangential velocity. In Fig. 15 we compare with $v_{\text{tan}}$ profiles provided by Baldi et al. [10] and Altamura et al. [5].

title: Benchmarking Quantum Neural Networks Developed for MBHB Coalescence in the Context of LISA Space Mission
authors: Maria-Catalina Isfan, Laurentiu-Ioan Caramete, Ana Caramete
abstract: Machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly explored to analyse gravitational wave (GW) data expected from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). At the same time, advances in quantum computing have stimulated interest in quantum machine learning as a potential alternative to conventional approaches. We investigate the applicability of quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and classical ML models to two tasks relevant for LISA observations of massive black hole binaries: GW signal detection and merger prediction. Using the Sangria dataset from the LISA Data Challenge, we benchmark several quantum architectures, including variational quantum classifiers (VQCs), post VQC hybrid models, quantum kernel methods, data reuploading classifiers, and quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) networks, against classical support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and LSTM networks. The models are trained on labelled data derived from the Sangria training dataset and evaluated on the corresponding blind dataset. For signal detection, several quantum models match or outperform classical baselines. In particular, the best performing hybrid post VQC architecture correctly identifies all signal samples in the blind dataset, while the standard VQC and data reuploading classifier achieve competitive detection rates. For merger detection and coalescence time estimation, however, the standard VQC emerges as the most reliable model, successfully localising all detected merger events with the lowest localisation errors. We further analyse the trade-offs between predictive performance, model complexity, and quantum circuit resources. Our results indicate that, although no universal quantum advantage is observed, selected quantum models can provide practical benefits for specific GW analysis tasks and represent promising candidates for future LISA data analysis pipelines.
comments: Submitted to Classical and Quantum Gravity

title: Channelled versus Isotropic Accretion of Galaxy Groups onto Clusters: Kinematics, Spin Alignment, and Assembly Bias
authors: Ankit Singh, Frazer Pearce, Meghan Gray, Ulrike Kuchner, Julian Onions, Gustavo Yepes, Alexander Knebe
abstract: Galaxy clusters grow by accreting groups from the cosmic web, but whether the route of infall (along a cluster-connected filament or from the open field) imprints a group's kinematics, spin, and orbit remains unmeasured at scale. We classify $212{,}704$ group-cluster infall pairs across $27{,}029$ clusters in the $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 simulation into primary (cluster-connected), secondary (tributary), primary-outskirt, and isotropic channels using DisPerSE filaments. (i) In both channelled classes, group spin axes lie mainly parallel to the filament below a `spin-flip' mass and perpendicular above it, $\log_{10} M_\mathrm{flip}\;[h^{-1}\,M_{\odot}] = 13.07$ and $13.12$, a $0.05$-dex offset consistent with zero, lying $1.3-1.4$ dex above the field, while isotropic groups show no flip; $M_\mathrm{flip}$ stays radially flat out to $7\,R_{200}$. (ii) Within the primary class $M_\mathrm{flip}$ rises with the linear mass density of the host filament, from $12.96$ (thin tendrils) to $13.44$ (dense bridges); matching group mass, cluster mass and distance keeps the rise positive but leaves its size uncertain ($0.07-0.58$ dex). (iii) Isotropic groups fall below random alignment at $2\,R_{200}$ ($41$ per cent within $60^\circ$, a $4.3\sigma$ deficit). Primary groups show $85$ per cent velocity-filament alignment at $2\,R_{200}$, and isotropic groups infall $150-180\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ faster, and more radially, out to $5\,R_{200}$. At matched distance isotropic groups are therefore predicted to reach orbital pericentres up to $10$ per cent smaller than primary groups, whose smaller pooled pericentres reflect only their proximity to the cluster. The topological route of accretion, and within it the host filament's linear density, shapes how groups enter clusters, testable with wide-area spectroscopic surveys.
